name: AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Professional
audience: Solutions architects with 2+ years designing and deploying cloud architecture on AWS
format: 75 items (65 scored, 10 unscored) in 180 minutes; multiple choice (1 correct of 4) and multiple response (2 or more correct of 5 or more, all must be chosen for credit); compensatory scoring with no penalty for guessing; scaled score 100–1000, pass 750. lessons.title: Hybrid and multi-VPC network connectivity
lessons.summary: Choose between VPC peering, Transit Gateway, PrivateLink, Direct Connect and Site-to-Site VPN, and design DNS that works across on-premises and AWS.

sections.heading: Pick the right VPC-to-VPC pattern
sections.body:
- **VPC peering** is a one-to-one link. It is **not transitive**: if A peers with B and B peers with C, A still cannot reach C. A full mesh grows as n(n-1)/2 links, so it gets hard to manage past a handful of VPCs.
- **AWS Transit Gateway (TGW)** is a Regional layer-3 virtual router. Attachments can be VPCs, Site-to-Site VPN, Direct Connect gateways, TGW Connect (GRE/BGP for SD-WAN appliances) and peering to other transit gateways. Use route tables on the TGW to segment traffic (for example, prod cannot reach dev).
- **AWS PrivateLink** exposes one *service* (behind a Network Load Balancer) to consumer VPCs through interface endpoints. Traffic flows one way, consumer to provider. Overlapping CIDRs do not matter, and the consumer never gets routes into the provider VPC.
- **Shared VPC (RAM subnet sharing)** lets a central network account own the VPC while application accounts launch resources into shared subnets.

sections.heading: Transit Gateway details that show up in scenarios
sections.body:
- **Inter-Region TGW peering supports static routes only** and does not support ECMP. Add static routes that point at the peering attachment.
- **Appliance mode** on the inspection VPC attachment pins both directions of a flow to the same AZ. Without it, a centralized stateful firewall can see asymmetric traffic and drop it.
- Route selection: a static route beats a propagated route for the same prefix. Between a Direct Connect gateway route and a VPN route for the same prefix, **the DX route is preferred** and the VPN is the backup.
- One Direct Connect gateway supports ECMP across multiple transit VIFs. AWS recommends using a single DX gateway.

sections.heading: Direct Connect resiliency
sections.body:
The Direct Connect Resiliency Toolkit describes these models:

| Model | Layout | SLA |
|---|---|---|
| Maximum resiliency | Separate connections on separate devices in **more than one location** | 99.99% |
| High resiliency | Single connections into multiple locations | 99.9% |
| Development and test | Separate devices in **one location** | No location-failure protection |

A Site-to-Site VPN over the internet is a common low-cost backup for DX. Use the toolkit's failover test to prove that failover works.

sections.heading: Hybrid DNS with Route 53 VPC Resolver
sections.body:
Route 53 Resolver was renamed **Route 53 VPC Resolver** when Route 53 Global Resolver was introduced. It answers at the VPC base address +2.

- **Inbound endpoint**: on-premises DNS servers forward queries for AWS names (such as private hosted zones) to IP addresses in your VPC.
- **Outbound endpoint + forwarding rules**: VPC workloads resolve on-premises domains such as corp.example.internal by forwarding to on-premises DNS servers.
- Share forwarding rules with other accounts through **AWS RAM**, so every spoke VPC uses one central set of endpoints. Both directions work over DX or VPN.

sections.heading: IP address planning
sections.body: Plan non-overlapping IPv4 ranges for everything that must route to everything else, including on-premises networks. Overlaps block peering and TGW routing between the overlapping networks. PrivateLink is the usual workaround when you cannot re-IP. A central IP address manager such as VPC IPAM helps allocate ranges per account and Region. For IPv6, AWS assigns globally unique ranges, so overlap is not the problem. Instead, plan dual-stack routing and use egress-only internet gateways for outbound-only IPv6.

keyPoints: VPC peering is non-transitive. Transit Gateway is the hub for many VPCs plus hybrid links.
TGW peering uses static routes only. Appliance mode keeps stateful inspection symmetric.
With equal prefixes on a TGW, DX routes are preferred over VPN routes.
Maximum DX resiliency means separate devices in more than one location.
Inbound Resolver endpoints serve on-premises queries for AWS names. Outbound endpoints plus rules serve VPC queries for on-premises names.
PrivateLink publishes a single service and works across overlapping CIDRs.

gotchas.trap: Adding a peering link between hub and spokes to make traffic transit through the hub VPC.
gotchas.correct: Peering is never transitive. Use Transit Gateway, or peer each pair directly.

gotchas.trap: Enabling route propagation across an inter-Region TGW peering attachment.
gotchas.correct: TGW peering supports only static routes. Add static routes that point at the peering attachment.

gotchas.trap: Two DX connections on two devices in the same location count as maximum resiliency.
gotchas.correct: That is the development and test model. Maximum resiliency needs more than one location.

gotchas.trap: Using an outbound Resolver endpoint so on-premises servers can resolve a private hosted zone.
gotchas.correct: On-premises to AWS needs an inbound endpoint. Outbound endpoints are for AWS to on-premises.

lessons.lab:
1. In a sandbox account, create three VPCs with non-overlapping CIDRs and a Transit Gateway with two route tables (shared and isolated).
2. Attach the VPCs and use associations and propagations so that VPC A and VPC B can each reach VPC C but not each other.
3. Create a Route 53 VPC Resolver outbound endpoint and a forwarding rule for a test domain. Share the rule through AWS RAM to a second account and associate it with a VPC there.
4. Delete the TGW attachments, endpoints and TGW when you finish to avoid hourly charges.

lessons.title: Security controls across many accounts
lessons.summary: Layer IAM Identity Center, SCPs, RCPs, permissions boundaries, KMS key policies and organization-wide detective services into one consistent control plan.

sections.heading: Workforce identity with IAM Identity Center
sections.body: IAM Identity Center is the central place to give the workforce access to many accounts. Connect an external identity provider over **SAML 2.0**, and use **SCIM** to sync users and groups automatically. **Permission sets** become IAM roles in each assigned account. Assign permission sets to groups, not individuals, and use attributes for ABAC where it fits.

sections.heading: Guardrails: SCPs and RCPs
sections.body:
- **Service control policies (SCPs)** set the maximum permissions for *principals* in member accounts.
- **Resource control policies (RCPs)** set the maximum permissions on *resources* in member accounts, including access by principals **outside** the organization. This makes them a data-perimeter tool.
- Neither type **grants** anything. Effective access is the intersection of SCPs, RCPs, identity policies and resource policies.
- Neither SCPs nor RCPs affect the **management account**. RCPs do apply to delegated-administrator member accounts. They do not restrict service-linked roles and do not apply to AWS managed KMS keys.
- RCPs need **all features** enabled and cover only a subset of services (for example S3, STS, KMS, SQS, Secrets Manager). Test them on a test OU before attaching them at the root.

sections.heading: Delegating safely with permissions boundaries
sections.body: A **permissions boundary** is a managed policy that sets the maximum permissions an IAM role or user can ever have. A common pattern lets developers create roles only if they attach a specific boundary (enforced with a condition on iam:PermissionsBoundary). They also must not be able to edit or remove that boundary. This stops privilege escalation without a central team having to review every role.

sections.heading: Encryption and secrets across accounts
sections.body:
- To use a **KMS customer managed key** from another account, you need **both** of these: the key policy in the owning account must allow the other account (or a specific role in it), and an IAM policy in the other account must allow the KMS actions on that key ARN.
- AWS managed keys (aws/service) cannot be shared across accounts. Cross-account use needs a customer managed key.
- **Secrets Manager** handles rotation, for example for database credentials. To share a secret across accounts, add a resource policy to the secret **and** encrypt it with a customer managed key whose key policy allows the consumer.

sections.heading: Organization-wide detection
sections.body: Register a **delegated administrator** (usually a security-tooling account) for GuardDuty and Security Hub, and turn on auto-enable so new accounts are covered. Security Hub was split. **AWS Security Hub CSPM** is the posture service with standards checks and ASFF findings. The newer **AWS Security Hub** correlates findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Security Hub CSPM, Macie and others into prioritized exposures. Use cross-Region aggregation so one account and Region shows the whole estate.

keyPoints: IAM Identity Center + external IdP (SAML + SCIM) + permission sets is the standard way to give a workforce multi-account access.
SCPs limit principals, RCPs limit resources. Neither grants permissions or affects the management account.
Permissions boundaries let teams create their own roles without escalating privileges.
Cross-account KMS needs both the key policy and the caller's IAM policy to allow it.
Run GuardDuty and Security Hub from a delegated administrator account with auto-enable turned on.

gotchas.trap: Attaching an SCP that allows s3:* to give a team S3 access.
gotchas.correct: SCPs never grant. The team still needs an identity-based policy.

gotchas.trap: Expecting an RCP at the root to protect buckets in the management account.
gotchas.correct: RCPs do not affect the management account. Keep workloads out of it.

gotchas.trap: Sharing a secret encrypted with the aws/secretsmanager key with another account.
gotchas.correct: Use a customer managed KMS key that the consumer account is allowed to use.

gotchas.trap: Running security services from the management account.
gotchas.correct: Delegate administration to a dedicated security account.

lessons.lab:
1. In a test organization with all features enabled, create a Sandbox OU and attach an SCP that denies organizations:LeaveOrganization and cloudtrail:StopLogging.
2. Attach an RCP to the same OU that denies S3 access unless aws:PrincipalOrgID matches your organization. Confirm that an external principal is blocked even when a bucket policy allows it.
3. Create a role whose permissions boundary allows only S3 and CloudWatch Logs. Confirm that attaching AdministratorAccess to it still does not let it call EC2.
4. Detach the test policies when you finish.

lessons.title: Resilient multi-AZ and multi-Region designs
lessons.summary: Match DR strategies to RTO/RPO and budget, choose data replication, and fail over with data-plane mechanisms.

sections.heading: RTO, RPO and the four strategies
sections.body:
**RTO** is how long the business can be down. **RPO** is how much data, measured in time, it can lose. Strategies, from cheapest to most expensive:

| Strategy | What runs in the recovery Region | Typical fit |
|---|---|---|
| Backup and restore | Backups only. Infrastructure is redeployed with IaC. | Hours of RTO/RPO, lowest cost |
| Pilot light | Data stores live and replicating. App tier switched off, ideally not deployed. | Tens of minutes. Cannot serve traffic until you act. |
| Warm standby | Scaled-down but fully working stack | Minutes. Takes traffic at once, then scales up. |
| Multi-site active/active | Full stack serving traffic in each Region | Near-zero RTO, highest cost |

Hot standby is the active/passive variant: a full-capacity, statically stable copy that does not serve traffic until failover.

sections.heading: Backup and restore realities
sections.body: AWS Backup can copy backups across Regions and accounts, but it has **no scheduled or automatic restore**. You automate restore yourself (for example with SNS + Lambda) and redeploy infrastructure from CloudFormation or CDK. AMIs and configuration must also be in the recovery Region. A separate DR account per Region adds isolation.

sections.heading: Continuous replication options
sections.body:
- S3 Cross-Region Replication (optionally with S3 Replication Time Control)
- RDS cross-Region read replicas
- **Aurora Global Database**: up to five secondary Regions, typical lag under one second. **Switchover** (formerly managed planned failover) gives RPO 0 for planned moves. **Failover** with allow-data-loss is for real outages and has a non-zero RPO. Applications should use the global writer endpoint.
- DynamoDB global tables (multi-Region, multi-writer, last writer wins)
- DocumentDB global clusters and ElastiCache Global Datastore

Active/active write patterns: **write global** (one writer Region, such as Aurora Global Database with write forwarding), **write local** (DynamoDB global tables), and **write partitioned** (for example, bidirectional S3 replication).

sections.heading: Fail over with the data plane
sections.body: During a Regional event, control-plane APIs are the parts most likely to be impaired. AWS recommends failing over with **data-plane** mechanisms: Route 53 health checks with failover records, and **Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC)** routing controls. Changing weighted-record weights or Global Accelerator traffic dials are **control-plane** operations. Warm standby that depends on Auto Scaling to add capacity also depends on the control plane. CloudFront origin failover works per request.

sections.heading: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery
sections.body: Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) continuously replicates servers at the block level from almost any source into a low-cost staging area, in a pilot-light style, and launches recovery instances on demand. For workloads already on AWS it protects **EC2 instances, not RDS**. Pair it with native database replication or AWS Backup copies.

keyPoints: Cost and recovery speed rise together: backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby, active/active.
Pilot light cannot serve traffic until you act. Warm standby can serve right away at reduced capacity.
Aurora Global Database switchover = RPO 0 for planned events. Failover = non-zero RPO for outages.
Fail over with data-plane controls: Route 53 health checks and ARC routing controls.
Active/active still needs backups, because corruption replicates too.
DRS protects EC2 and servers, not RDS.

gotchas.trap: Pilot light gives near-zero RTO because the database is already running.
gotchas.correct: The app tier must be deployed or started first. Choose warm standby or active/active for minutes or less.

gotchas.trap: Failing over by calling the Route 53 API to change record weights.
gotchas.correct: That is a control-plane change. Pre-provision health-checked failover records or ARC routing controls.

gotchas.trap: AWS Backup will automatically restore in the DR Region on a schedule.
gotchas.correct: AWS Backup has no automatic restore. Script it and test it.

gotchas.trap: Active/active means you no longer need backups.
gotchas.correct: Replication copies corruption and deletes. Keep point-in-time backups.

lessons.lab:
1. Create an Aurora Global Database with a secondary Region in a sandbox.
2. Perform a switchover and note that the global writer endpoint follows the new primary.
3. Create two Route 53 failover records with a health check and stop the primary endpoint to watch DNS move to the secondary.
4. Delete the global cluster and health checks afterward.

lessons.title: Multi-account environments with Organizations and Control Tower
lessons.summary: Structure OUs, build a governed landing zone with Control Tower, and share resources across accounts.

sections.heading: Why many accounts
sections.body: An account is the strongest isolation boundary in AWS. It separates blast radius, quotas, billing and permissions. **AWS Organizations** groups accounts into **organizational units (OUs)**. It provides consolidated billing, delegated administration for services, policy types (SCPs, RCPs, tag policies, backup policies, chat applications policies) and resource sharing through **AWS RAM**, such as VPC subnets and Resolver rules. Keep the management account free of workloads, because SCPs and RCPs do not restrict it.

sections.heading: Typical OU layout
sections.body:
- **Security OU**: log archive account (org CloudTrail trail and Config data) and security tooling account (delegated admin for GuardDuty and Security Hub).
- **Infrastructure OU**: shared networking (Transit Gateway, DX, central egress and inspection) and shared services.
- **Workloads OU** split into prod and non-prod, plus **Sandbox** and **Suspended** OUs.

Attach guardrails at the OU level so new accounts inherit them automatically.

sections.heading: AWS Control Tower
sections.body:
Control Tower sets up a landing zone by orchestrating Organizations, IAM Identity Center and Service Catalog. **Account Factory** provisions standardized accounts as Service Catalog products. Controls come in three behaviors:

- **Preventive**: block actions (implemented with SCPs or RCPs).
- **Detective**: find noncompliant resources after the fact (implemented with AWS Config rules).
- **Proactive**: check resources *before* they are provisioned (CloudFormation hooks).

Controls are grouped as mandatory, strongly recommended or elective. Control Tower detects drift, and you can register an existing organization's OUs and enroll existing accounts.

sections.heading: Deploying baselines everywhere
sections.body: Use **CloudFormation StackSets** with service-managed permissions to deploy roles, Config rules or logging into every account and Region in an OU, with automatic deployment for new accounts. Pair that with an organization CloudTrail trail and Config aggregation into the log archive and security accounts.

keyPoints: Accounts are the isolation boundary. OUs are how you apply policy at scale.
Keep the management account for billing and organization administration only.
Control Tower = landing zone + Account Factory + preventive, detective and proactive controls.
Use RAM to share TGWs, subnets and Resolver rules instead of duplicating them.
Use StackSets with auto-deployment to apply baselines to new accounts.

gotchas.trap: Running production workloads in the management account to save an account.
gotchas.correct: SCPs and RCPs cannot restrict that account. Move workloads to member accounts.

gotchas.trap: Using a detective control to stop a noncompliant resource from being created.
gotchas.correct: Detective controls only report. Use preventive or proactive controls to block.

gotchas.trap: You must rebuild your organization to adopt Control Tower.
gotchas.correct: You can register existing OUs and enroll existing accounts.

lessons.lab:
1. In a sandbox organization, sketch an OU tree with Security, Infrastructure, Workloads/Prod, Workloads/NonProd, Sandbox and Suspended OUs.
2. If you have a Control Tower test environment, turn on one strongly recommended detective control and one proactive control on the NonProd OU, then try to deploy a noncompliant stack.
3. Create a StackSet with service-managed permissions and automatic deployment targeting the Sandbox OU. Move a test account into the OU and confirm that the stack appears.

lessons.title: Cost visibility and chargeback across an organization
lessons.summary: Attribute spend to business units with accounts, tags and cost categories, and control it with budgets, anomaly detection and commitment sharing.

sections.heading: Attribution building blocks
sections.body:
- **Accounts** are the cleanest unit of attribution. Spend in one account maps to one owner.
- **Cost allocation tags** (for example CostCenter, Project) must be **activated in the management (payer) account** before they show in Cost Explorer and billing data. By default they apply from activation onward, so activate them early (AWS also offers a limited backfill of past months on request).
- **Tag policies** in Organizations standardize tag keys and values. Combine them with SCPs or proactive controls to require tags at creation.
- **AWS Cost Categories** map accounts, tags and services into business groupings. **Split charge rules** spread shared costs, such as a central networking account, across the consuming categories.

sections.heading: Reporting and guardrails
sections.body:
- **Cost Explorer** handles interactive analysis and forecasting. **Cost and Usage Reports (CUR / Data Exports)** provide line-item detail you can query with Athena or load into BI tools for chargeback.
- **AWS Budgets** sends alerts (and can run actions) when actual or forecast spend crosses a threshold, scoped per account, tag or cost category.
- **Cost Anomaly Detection** uses machine learning to flag unusual spend patterns.
- **Trusted Advisor** and **Compute Optimizer** surface right-sizing and idle resources.

sections.heading: Commitments in an organization
sections.body: With consolidated billing, Reserved Instance and Savings Plans discounts are **shared across accounts** in the organization by default. The management account can turn sharing off for specific accounts, for example when a business unit that bought commitments must keep the benefit for chargeback. Buying commitments centrally and spreading the benefit usually raises overall utilization.

keyPoints: Activate cost allocation tags in the management account, and do it early: by default they do not cover spend from before activation.
Use Cost Categories with split charge rules to allocate shared platform costs.
Use CUR / Data Exports for line-item chargeback and Cost Explorer for analysis.
Use Budgets for thresholds and Cost Anomaly Detection for unexpected spikes.
RI and Savings Plans discounts are shared across the organization by default. Sharing can be turned off per account.

gotchas.trap: Applying a tag to resources is enough for it to appear in Cost Explorer.
gotchas.correct: The tag must also be activated as a cost allocation tag in the payer account.

gotchas.trap: Expecting tags activated today to recategorize last quarter's spend.
gotchas.correct: By default tags apply from activation onward. Activate them early, and use account structure or Cost Categories for a clean historical view.

gotchas.trap: Duplicating a Transit Gateway per business unit just to split its cost.
gotchas.correct: Keep it shared and allocate it with Cost Categories split charge rules.

lessons.lab:
1. In the management account, open Billing and Cost Management and activate a CostCenter user-defined tag as a cost allocation tag.
2. Create a Cost Category that maps two accounts to BU-A and BU-B, and add a split charge rule that spreads a shared-services account proportionally.
3. Create a monthly budget scoped to BU-A with a forecast-based alert.

lessons.title: Deployment strategies: IaC, CI/CD and safe releases
lessons.summary: Use CloudFormation, CDK and StackSets to make environments repeatable, then pick a release pattern (rolling, blue/green, canary, linear) that matches the blast radius and rollback speed the business needs.

sections.heading: Infrastructure as code is the default
sections.body:
For a new solution, every environment should come from templates, not console clicks.

- **AWS CloudFormation** declares resources in a template and manages them as a **stack**. **Change sets** show what an update will add, modify or *replace* before you run it. **Drift detection** finds changes made outside CloudFormation.
- **AWS CDK** lets you define infrastructure in a programming language. `cdk synth` produces CloudFormation templates, so the deployment engine is still CloudFormation. **Aspects** can visit every construct in a CDK app, for example to enforce encryption.
- **StackSets** deploy one template to many accounts and Regions in a single operation. With service-managed permissions through AWS Organizations, a StackSet can deploy automatically to new accounts added to a target OU.
- **CloudFormation Hooks** check resources *before* they are provisioned, for any stack, whatever tool wrote the template. AWS Config rules are detective: they evaluate resources after they exist.

sections.heading: Protecting stateful resources
sections.body:
- `DeletionPolicy` (`Retain`, `Snapshot` where supported, or `Delete`) controls what happens when a resource is removed from the template or the stack is deleted.
- `UpdateReplacePolicy` controls what happens to the *old* physical resource when an update forces replacement, for example after you change an immutable property.
- **Stack policies** block updates to named resources unless they are explicitly overridden. **Termination protection** stops someone deleting the whole stack.
- **Rollback triggers** let CloudFormation watch CloudWatch alarms during a create or update and roll back if an alarm fires.
- Never put secrets in templates or parameters files. Use **dynamic references** (`{{resolve:secretsmanager:...}}`) or let the service manage the secret, for example the RDS managed master user password in Secrets Manager.

sections.heading: CI/CD building blocks
sections.body:
- **CodePipeline** orchestrates stages. **CodeBuild** builds and tests. **CodeDeploy** deploys to EC2/on-premises, Lambda and ECS. **CodeCommit** is open to new customers again (it returned to general availability in November 2025), but pipelines can also use third-party Git providers.
- **Cross-account pipelines** usually run in a tooling account and assume a deployment role in each target account. The artifact bucket must be encrypted with a **customer managed KMS key** whose key policy allows the target accounts, because an AWS managed key cannot be shared across accounts.
- Add manual approval actions, automated tests and security scans (for example Amazon Inspector and ECR image scanning) as pipeline gates.

sections.heading: Choosing a release pattern
sections.body:
| Pattern | How it works | Rollback | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|---|
| All-at-once / in-place | Update every target together | Redeploy the old version | Fast and cheap, but the biggest blast radius |
| Rolling | Replace in batches | Roll forward or back batch by batch | Mixed versions run at the same time |
| Blue/green | Build a full new environment, then switch traffic | Switch back to blue | Needs double capacity for a while |
| Canary | Small slice of traffic first, then the rest | Shift the slice back | Needs good metrics and alarms |
| Linear | Shift equal increments at fixed intervals | Shift back | Slower, but steady |

- **Lambda**: CodeDeploy shifts traffic between alias versions with predefined canary, linear or all-at-once configurations and rolls back automatically when a CloudWatch alarm fires. AWS SAM exposes this as `DeploymentPreference`.
- **ECS**: CodeDeploy blue/green uses two target groups, a production listener and an optional **test listener** so you can validate green before it takes production traffic. The ECS **deployment circuit breaker** can roll back a failed rolling deployment automatically.
- **EC2**: CodeDeploy blue/green can create replacement instances (for example a copy of the Auto Scaling group) and keep the original instances for a fast rollback.
- DNS-based switching (Route 53 weighted records) works, but clients cache DNS, so cut-over and rollback are slower and less precise than switching at a load balancer or alias.

keyPoints: CDK synthesizes to CloudFormation. StackSets fan a template out to many accounts and Regions.
Change sets preview updates. Drift detection finds out-of-band changes. Hooks block non-compliant resources before provisioning.
Use DeletionPolicy and UpdateReplacePolicy (Retain or Snapshot) on databases and other stateful resources.
Cross-account pipelines need a customer managed KMS key on the artifact bucket and assumable roles in the target accounts.
Canary and linear traffic shifting with alarm-based automatic rollback are built into CodeDeploy for Lambda and ECS.

gotchas.trap: Drift detection will warn me before an update replaces my database.
gotchas.correct: Drift detection compares live resources with the template. A change set shows planned replacements before you run the update.

gotchas.trap: NoEcho parameters make it safe to keep passwords in parameter files.
gotchas.correct: NoEcho only masks the value in output. Use dynamic references to Secrets Manager, or let RDS manage the master password.

gotchas.trap: Route 53 weighted records give instant blue/green rollback.
gotchas.correct: Clients and resolvers cache DNS for the TTL. Switching at the load balancer or Lambda alias is faster and more precise.

gotchas.trap: AWS Config rules prevent non-compliant stacks from deploying.
gotchas.correct: Config rules are detective. Use CloudFormation Hooks (or Control Tower proactive controls) to stop resources before they are provisioned.

lessons.lab: Write a small CDK app with one Lambda function behind an alias. Synthesize it and read the generated CloudFormation template. Add a CodeDeploy canary deployment that is tied to a CloudWatch error alarm. Deploy a version that throws errors and watch the automatic rollback. Finally, change an immutable property on a test RDS instance and review the change set to see the planned replacement.

lessons.title: Business continuity: RTO, RPO and DR strategy for new workloads
lessons.summary: Turn business RTO and RPO targets into a DR strategy, a data replication choice and a failover mechanism that relies on the data plane.

sections.heading: Start from RTO and RPO
sections.body:
- **RTO** (recovery time objective): the longest acceptable time to restore service.
- **RPO** (recovery point objective): the most data loss you can accept, measured in time.

Lower targets cost more. Pick the cheapest strategy that meets both numbers, and remember that **high availability (Multi-AZ) and disaster recovery (multi-Region or multi-account) are different problems**. Multi-AZ protects against losing a data center. It does not protect against a Regional event, a bad deployment or corrupted data.

sections.heading: The four DR strategies
sections.body:
| Strategy | What runs in the recovery Region | RTO / RPO | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Backup and restore | Backups only. Redeploy infrastructure with IaC | Hours | Lowest |
| Pilot light | Data stores live and replicating. App tier switched off or not deployed | Tens of minutes. RPO from replication | Low |
| Warm standby | Scaled-down but fully working copy that can take traffic at once | Minutes | Medium |
| Multi-site active/active | Full production in each Region | Near zero RTO | Highest |

- Pilot light **cannot serve traffic until you act** (deploy or start the app tier). Warm standby can serve traffic right away and only needs to scale up.
- Active/active still needs backups. Replication copies corruption and accidental deletes too, so the RPO for those events is not zero.
- **AWS Backup** supports cross-Region and cross-account copies, but it has no scheduled automatic restore. Automate restores yourself if the plan needs them.
- **AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery** does continuous block-level replication into a low-cost staging area (a pilot-light model). For workloads already on AWS it covers EC2, not RDS.

sections.heading: Data replication options
sections.body:
- **RDS Multi-AZ**: synchronous standby in another AZ with automatic failover. This is HA, not cross-Region DR.
- **Read replicas** (including cross-Region): asynchronous, and you promote them yourself.
- **Aurora Global Database**: storage-based replication to up to five secondary Regions, typically under a second of lag. **Switchover** (formerly managed planned failover) is for planned moves with RPO 0. **Failover** is for real outages and can lose recent data.
- **DynamoDB global tables**: multi-active replicas so each Region can write locally ("write local", last writer wins by default).
- **S3 Cross-Region Replication**, optionally with Replication Time Control for a predictable replication time.
- **ElastiCache Global Datastore** and **DocumentDB global clusters** cover caches and document data.

sections.heading: Fail over with the data plane
sections.body:
During an event, control planes (APIs that create or change resources) are more likely to be impaired than data planes. AWS guidance is to **fail over using data-plane operations**.

- Route 53 **health checks** and **Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) routing controls** act on the data plane.
- Editing weighted record weights, changing Global Accelerator traffic dials, or depending on Auto Scaling to launch capacity are control-plane actions.
- **Static stability**: pre-provision enough capacity that losing an AZ (or Region, for hot standby) needs no new resources. For example, if you need six instances and want to survive the loss of one of three AZs, run three per AZ (nine in total).
- Protect backups from ransomware and insiders with **AWS Backup Vault Lock**, **S3 Object Lock** and copies in a separate, locked-down account.

keyPoints: RTO = time to recover. RPO = acceptable data loss. Pick the cheapest strategy that meets both.
Pilot light needs action before it can serve traffic. Warm standby can serve right away at reduced scale.
Aurora Global Database switchover gives RPO 0 for planned moves. Failover accepts some data loss.
Fail over with data-plane mechanisms such as Route 53 health checks and ARC routing controls.
Static stability means pre-provisioned capacity, not relying on scaling during the event.

gotchas.trap: Multi-AZ RDS is a disaster recovery plan.
gotchas.correct: Multi-AZ is high availability inside one Region. Cross-Region DR needs replicas, global databases or backup copies in another Region.

gotchas.trap: Active/active means RPO is zero for every kind of failure.
gotchas.correct: Replication also copies corruption and deletes. You still need point-in-time backups.

gotchas.trap: Elastic Disaster Recovery can protect our RDS databases.
gotchas.correct: For AWS-hosted sources it replicates EC2 instances. Use database-native replication or AWS Backup for RDS.

gotchas.trap: We will fail over by editing Route 53 weights during the outage.
gotchas.correct: That is a control-plane change. Pre-configure health checks or ARC routing controls so failover uses the data plane.

lessons.lab: Build a two-Region pilot light: an Aurora Global Database (or a cross-Region read replica), an S3 bucket with CRR, and a CloudFormation template for the app tier that is not deployed in the secondary Region. Add Route 53 failover records with health checks. Time a full recovery drill and compare the measured RTO and RPO with the targets.

lessons.title: Designing reliable architectures: decoupling, routing and recovery
lessons.summary: Build reliability into a new design with loose coupling, idempotent consumers, retries with backoff, health-checked routing and the right edge or DNS service.

sections.heading: Loose coupling absorbs spikes
sections.body:
- Put a queue (**Amazon SQS**) between producers and consumers so bursts are buffered instead of overloading the backend. Scale consumers on queue backlog.
- SQS standard queues deliver **at least once** and do not guarantee order, so consumers must be **idempotent**. FIFO queues give ordering and deduplication within limits.
- Use **SNS** or **EventBridge** for fan-out and event routing. Use **Step Functions** for multi-step workflows with retries and error handling: **Standard** workflows suit long-running, exactly-once orchestration (up to a year); **Express** workflows suit high-volume, short (up to five minutes) at-least-once processing.
- Use dead-letter queues so poison messages do not block processing.

sections.heading: Retries, timeouts and circuit breakers
sections.body:
- Retry transient errors with **exponential backoff and jitter**, and cap the number of retries. Immediate, synchronized retries cause retry storms.
- Set timeouts on every remote call.
- A **circuit breaker** stops calling a failing dependency for a while so it can recover. Bulkheads isolate resources so one failure does not drain everything.
- Throttle at the front door (API Gateway throttling and usage plans) to protect the backend.

sections.heading: Routing traffic reliably
sections.body:
| Need | Service / policy |
|---|---|
| Active/passive between endpoints | Route 53 **failover** routing with health checks |
| Lowest latency Region per user | Route 53 **latency** routing |
| Route by user location (compliance, localization) | Route 53 **geolocation** (or geoproximity with bias) |
| Gradual shift or A/B | Route 53 **weighted** routing |
| Static anycast IPs, fast failover, TCP/UDP | **AWS Global Accelerator** |
| Cache HTTP(S) content at the edge | **Amazon CloudFront** (origin failover works per request) |

- Route 53 health checkers run on the public internet. To check a private resource, base the health check on a **CloudWatch alarm**.
- Global Accelerator does not depend on client DNS caching for failover, which makes it a good fit for non-HTTP or latency-sensitive traffic.

sections.heading: Multi-AZ by default
sections.body:
- Spread Auto Scaling groups, load balancers and data stores across at least two AZs, and three for static stability.
- Prefer managed, Multi-AZ services (Aurora, DynamoDB, S3, EFS, SQS, Lambda) to reduce the failure modes you operate yourself.
- Track dependencies: a Multi-AZ app with a single-AZ NAT gateway or cache still has a single point of failure.

keyPoints: Queues buffer load. Consumers of standard queues must be idempotent.
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter. Add timeouts and circuit breakers.
Route 53 failover, latency, geolocation and weighted policies solve different routing problems.
Use CloudWatch-alarm-based health checks for private endpoints.
Global Accelerator gives static anycast IPs and fast failover for TCP and UDP.

gotchas.trap: Latency routing keeps EU users in the EU for data residency.
gotchas.correct: Latency routing picks the fastest Region, which may not be in the EU. Use geolocation routing for location rules.

gotchas.trap: An SQS standard queue processes each message exactly once.
gotchas.correct: Standard queues are at-least-once. Design idempotent consumers or use FIFO deduplication where it fits.

gotchas.trap: Route 53 can health check an internal ALB directly.
gotchas.correct: Health checkers are on the internet. Use a CloudWatch alarm-based health check for private resources.

lessons.lab: Put an SQS queue with a dead-letter queue between an API Gateway endpoint and a Lambda consumer. Make the consumer idempotent with a DynamoDB conditional write keyed on the message ID. Send duplicate messages and a burst of load, then check that each order is stored only once and that backlog-based scaling keeps up.

lessons.title: Security controls for new workloads
lessons.summary: Design least-privilege identity, layered network controls, edge protection and encryption into a new workload from day one.

sections.heading: Identity and least privilege
sections.body:
- Give workloads **IAM roles** (instance profiles, Lambda execution roles, ECS task roles), never long-term access keys. Require IMDSv2 on EC2.
- Scope policies to specific actions and resources. Use conditions and, where useful, attribute-based access control (ABAC) with tags.
- **Amazon Cognito user pools** authenticate users and issue JWTs. **Identity pools** exchange identities for temporary AWS credentials. Policy variables such as `${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}` scope each user to their own S3 prefix.
- Org-level guardrails (SCPs, RCPs) and permissions boundaries limit what roles can do even if a policy is too broad.

sections.heading: Network controls
sections.body:
- **Security groups** are stateful and attached to ENIs. Reference other security groups (ALB SG to app SG to DB SG) instead of CIDR ranges.
- **Network ACLs** are stateless and apply to subnets. Return traffic needs explicit rules, usually the ephemeral port range.
- **VPC endpoints** keep traffic to AWS services private. **Gateway endpoints** (S3, DynamoDB) are free and use route tables. **Interface endpoints** (PrivateLink) put ENIs in your subnets for many other services. Endpoint policies restrict what can be reached.
- Use private subnets for app and data tiers. Expose only load balancers or CloudFront.

sections.heading: Edge and attack mitigation
sections.body:
- **CloudFront** plus **AWS WAF** filters layer 7 attacks. Use managed rule groups and **rate-based rules** to limit floods from single IPs.
- **AWS Shield Standard** is automatic and free. **Shield Advanced** adds DDoS response team support, enhanced detection and cost protection for scaling charges caused by an attack.
- **AWS Firewall Manager** applies WAF, Shield Advanced and security group policies across an organization.
- Restrict S3 origins to CloudFront with **origin access control (OAC)** and a bucket policy that names the distribution. Keep S3 Block Public Access on.
- CloudFront certificates from ACM must be requested in **us-east-1**.

sections.heading: Data protection and detection
sections.body:
- **AWS KMS customer managed keys** give you control of the key policy, rotation and grants. Separate key administrators from key users. CloudTrail records key use.
- **Secrets Manager** stores and rotates secrets (managed rotation for supported databases, or a Lambda rotation function). Parameter Store SecureString has no built-in rotation.
- **CloudHSM** is for single-tenant HSMs you control, when a requirement calls for it.
- Turn on detection from day one: **GuardDuty** (threat detection), **Inspector** (vulnerabilities), **Macie** (sensitive data in S3), and **AWS Security Hub CSPM** for posture checks. The newer **AWS Security Hub** (GA December 2025) correlates findings from these services. Use delegated administrators and auto-enable for new accounts.

keyPoints: Roles and temporary credentials everywhere. No long-term keys in code or on devices.
Security groups are stateful and can reference each other. NACLs are stateless.
Gateway endpoints for S3/DynamoDB, interface endpoints for other services, both with endpoint policies.
CloudFront + WAF rate-based rules for layer 7. Shield Advanced for response-team support and cost protection.
Secrets Manager rotates secrets. KMS customer managed keys give key-policy control.

gotchas.trap: A Cognito user pool gives the mobile app AWS credentials for S3.
gotchas.correct: User pools issue tokens. An identity pool exchanges them for temporary AWS credentials.

gotchas.trap: Adding an inbound NACL rule for 443 is enough for HTTPS.
gotchas.correct: NACLs are stateless. Outbound rules must allow return traffic on ephemeral ports.

gotchas.trap: An AWS managed KMS key can encrypt artifacts shared with another account.
gotchas.correct: You cannot edit an AWS managed key policy. Use a customer managed key for cross-account access.

gotchas.trap: Shield Standard includes the DDoS response team.
gotchas.correct: Response-team access and cost protection come with Shield Advanced.

lessons.lab: Build a three-tier VPC with an ALB security group, an app security group that allows traffic only from the ALB security group, and a database security group that allows traffic only from the app security group. Add a Secrets Manager secret with rotation for the database. Put CloudFront with AWS WAF and a rate-based rule in front, then load-test to see the rule block a single noisy IP.

lessons.title: Performance and cost: compute, storage, data, caching and purchasing
lessons.summary: Match compute, storage and database services to the access pattern, add caching where reads dominate, and pick purchasing options and network paths that cut cost without hurting reliability.

sections.heading: Compute: serverless, containers or EC2
sections.body:
| Choose | When |
|---|---|
| **Lambda** | Event-driven, short tasks (up to 15 minutes per invocation), spiky traffic, no servers to manage |
| **ECS/EKS on Fargate** | Containers, long-running or steady services, no host management |
| **ECS/EKS on EC2** | Need specific instance types, GPUs, daemon agents, or the best price at steady high use |
| **EC2 directly** | Licensing, OS-level control, or software that is not containerized |

- **Provisioned concurrency** removes Lambda cold starts for latency-sensitive paths. **Reserved concurrency** caps or guarantees a function's concurrency.
- Graviton (Arm) instances usually give better price performance when the software supports Arm.
- Lambda durable functions (December 2025) add checkpointed multi-step workflows inside Lambda. Step Functions remains the general orchestrator.

sections.heading: Storage and databases
sections.body:
- **EBS gp3**: IOPS and throughput are provisioned independently of size, usually cheaper than gp2. **io2** is for the most demanding, latency-sensitive databases. Instance store is fast but ephemeral.
- **EFS**: shared, elastic POSIX (NFS) file system across AZs for Linux. **FSx for Windows File Server**: SMB with Active Directory. **FSx for Lustre**: high-throughput HPC scratch or persistent storage that can link to S3. **FSx for NetApp ONTAP**: multiprotocol and NetApp features.
- **S3** storage classes and lifecycle rules. **Intelligent-Tiering** for unknown or changing access patterns.
- **Aurora** for high-performance relational workloads, **Aurora Serverless v2** for variable or intermittent load, **DynamoDB** for key-value at any scale (on-demand for unpredictable traffic, provisioned plus auto scaling for steady traffic).

sections.heading: Caching and buffering
sections.body:
- **CloudFront** caches at the edge and offloads origins. **Origin Shield** adds a central caching layer to reduce origin load further.
- **ElastiCache** (Redis OSS/Valkey or Memcached) caches query results and sessions. *Lazy loading* fills the cache on a miss; *write-through* updates it on every write.
- **DAX** is an in-memory cache for DynamoDB with microsecond reads through a DynamoDB-compatible API.
- **RDS Proxy** pools database connections, which protects RDS/Aurora from connection storms caused by many Lambda invocations.
- **Read replicas** scale reads. An RDS Multi-AZ instance standby does not serve reads.

sections.heading: Purchasing options and data transfer
sections.body:
| Option | Fits |
|---|---|
| On-Demand | Short-term, unpredictable, new workloads |
| **Compute Savings Plans** | Steady spend that may move across instance families, Regions, Fargate and Lambda |
| **EC2 Instance Savings Plans / Reserved Instances** | Steady use of a known instance family in one Region, for a deeper discount |
| **Spot** | Fault-tolerant, flexible work. Instances can be reclaimed with a two-minute notice |
| **Database Savings Plans** (December 2025) | Steady database spend across services such as Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB and ElastiCache, flexible across engine, family and Region (AWS cites savings of up to 35%) |

- Model data transfer: traffic from private subnets to S3 through a **NAT gateway** pays per-GB processing. An **S3 gateway endpoint** has no charge.
- Keep chatty components in the same AZ where reliability allows, and serve internet traffic through CloudFront.
- Prices, limits and discount levels change. Check the current pricing pages rather than memorizing numbers.

keyPoints: Lambda for short event-driven work, Fargate for containers without hosts, EC2 when you need control.
gp3 decouples IOPS from size. EFS is shared NFS, FSx for Lustre is HPC, FSx for Windows is SMB/AD.
CloudFront, ElastiCache and DAX cut latency and load. RDS Proxy absorbs Lambda connection storms.
Compute Savings Plans for flexible steady compute, Spot for interruptible work, Database Savings Plans for steady database spend.
Replace NAT gateway paths to S3 and DynamoDB with gateway endpoints.

gotchas.trap: RDS Multi-AZ standby can absorb read traffic.
gotchas.correct: An RDS Multi-AZ instance standby is not readable. Use read replicas or Aurora replicas for reads.

gotchas.trap: Provisioned concurrency fixes database connection exhaustion.
gotchas.correct: More warm Lambda environments can mean more connections. RDS Proxy pools them.

gotchas.trap: Run a 2-hour batch job in Lambda with the maximum timeout.
gotchas.correct: A single Lambda invocation is limited to 15 minutes. Use Fargate, AWS Batch or EC2 for long single tasks.

gotchas.trap: EBS Multi-Attach is a shared file system for many instances.
gotchas.correct: Multi-Attach is limited and needs a cluster-aware file system. Use EFS for shared POSIX storage.

lessons.lab: Take a sample Lambda + RDS API and load-test it until connections run out. Add RDS Proxy and repeat. Then put ElastiCache in front of the hottest query with lazy loading and measure latency. Finally, use the Pricing Calculator to compare On-Demand, Compute Savings Plans and Spot for the steady and batch parts of the workload.

lessons.title: Observability for Running Workloads
lessons.summary: How to turn an opaque production estate into one you can reason about: metrics, logs, traces, synthetic checks and cross-account visibility, and how to cut alarm noise.

sections.heading: The three signals and where they live
sections.body:
An existing workload usually has *some* monitoring. The improvement task is to close the gaps.

- **Metrics**: Amazon CloudWatch metrics. Use the CloudWatch agent for OS-level data such as memory and disk, which EC2 does not publish by default.
- **Logs**: CloudWatch Logs. **Metric filters** turn log patterns (for example, `ERROR` counts) into metrics you can alarm on. **Logs Insights** handles ad-hoc queries.
- **Traces**: AWS X-Ray, or the **AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT)** for vendor-neutral instrumentation. Use traces when latency is spread across many services and you need to know *which hop* is slow.

Container workloads add **Container Insights** for cluster, service and task metrics.

sections.heading: Outside-in monitoring
sections.body:
Internal metrics can all look green while users still fail.

- **CloudWatch Synthetics** canaries run scripted checks against endpoints and user journeys on a schedule. They catch outages *before* customers report them.
- **CloudWatch RUM** collects real browser-side performance and errors from actual users.
- **CloudWatch Application Signals** can define **SLOs** on service latency and availability, so alerting follows user-facing objectives rather than raw resource metrics.

sections.heading: Multi-account observability
sections.body:
In an AWS Organizations estate, engineers should not have to switch accounts to troubleshoot.

- **CloudWatch cross-account observability** links *source* accounts to a central *monitoring* account. From there you can view metrics, logs and traces across accounts.
- For long-term retention or analytics, use **CloudWatch Logs subscription filters** to stream logs to a central destination (for example, Amazon Data Firehose to an S3 bucket in a log-archive account).
- AWS CloudTrail **organization trails** capture API activity from every member account in one place.

sections.heading: Alarms that people trust
sections.body:
Alert fatigue is an operational-excellence defect.

- **Composite alarms** combine several alarms with AND/OR logic, so one actionable page replaces a storm of symptoms.
- **Anomaly detection** alarms learn a metric's expected band. Use them where a static threshold fits badly, such as seasonal traffic.
- Alarm on symptoms customers feel (error rate, latency percentiles, SLO burn) and use cause metrics for diagnosis.

keyPoints: EC2 memory and disk utilisation need the CloudWatch agent; they are not default EC2 metrics.
Metric filters convert log patterns into alarmable metrics.
X-Ray or ADOT traces locate the slow hop in a distributed request.
Synthetics canaries give outside-in detection; RUM gives real-user data.
Cross-account observability centralises viewing in a monitoring account; subscription filters centralise log storage.
Composite alarms cut noise by paging only when a meaningful combination of conditions holds.

gotchas.trap: Adding more static-threshold alarms to fix missed incidents.
gotchas.correct: Add outside-in checks (Synthetics), alarm on user-facing symptoms or SLOs, and use composite alarms to keep pages actionable.

gotchas.trap: Using CloudTrail to find which microservice adds latency.
gotchas.correct: CloudTrail records API calls for audit. Use distributed tracing (X-Ray/ADOT) for latency.

gotchas.trap: Copying IAM users into every account so operators can read dashboards.
gotchas.correct: Use CloudWatch cross-account observability with a central monitoring account.

lessons.lab: In a sandbox account, install the CloudWatch agent on an EC2 instance to publish memory metrics. Create a metric filter on an application log group for the string "ERROR", alarm on it, and combine that alarm with a CPU alarm in a composite alarm. Then add a Synthetics heartbeat canary against a public test endpoint and watch its success metric.

lessons.title: Automation and Incident Response
lessons.summary: Replacing manual operations with event-driven automation: Systems Manager runbooks, EventBridge rules, Config remediation, safe access and patching at scale.

sections.heading: Event-driven operations
sections.body:
The pattern behind most "improve operations" answers looks like this:

**signal → Amazon EventBridge rule (or CloudWatch alarm) → automated action**

Typical signals include GuardDuty findings, Config compliance changes, AWS Health events, CloudWatch alarm state changes and EC2 state changes. Typical actions are **Systems Manager Automation** runbooks, Lambda functions, Step Functions workflows or SNS notifications.

Prefer **managed runbooks** (Systems Manager Automation documents) over custom scripts on a cron host. Runbooks are versioned, auditable, can run across accounts and Regions, and support approval steps.

sections.heading: AWS Systems Manager toolbox
sections.body:
- **Session Manager**: shell access with no inbound ports, no bastion and no SSH keys. Access is controlled by IAM, and sessions can be logged to S3 or CloudWatch Logs.
- **Run Command**: run ad-hoc commands across a fleet.
- **State Manager**: keep instances in a defined configuration.
- **Patch Manager**: patch baselines plus maintenance windows, with compliance reporting. Patch policies through Quick Setup can apply across an organization.
- **Automation**: multi-step runbooks, including AWS-provided ones for common fixes.
- **Parameter Store**: configuration values.

sections.heading: Detecting and fixing drift
sections.body:
- **AWS Config** rules evaluate resource configuration continuously. A non-compliant result can trigger a **remediation action**, which is a Systems Manager Automation document. It runs either manually or automatically.
- **Conformance packs** bundle rules and remediations, and you can deploy them across an organization.
- **CloudFormation drift detection** shows where resources were changed outside the stack. The lasting fix is to update the template and make changes only through IaC.

sections.heading: Incident response basics
sections.body:
- Write response steps as runbooks *before* the incident and test them, for example with **AWS Fault Injection Service** experiments or game days.
- Route **AWS Health** events through EventBridge so scheduled maintenance and service events reach the owning team automatically.
- After an incident, feed the findings back into alarms, runbooks and architecture. That loop is the "continuous improvement" the domain is named for.

keyPoints: EventBridge plus Systems Manager Automation is the default pattern for replacing manual runbooks.
Session Manager removes bastions, open SSH ports and key management, and it logs sessions.
Patch Manager uses patch baselines and maintenance windows and reports compliance.
Config rules can trigger automatic remediation through SSM Automation documents.
CloudFormation drift detection finds out-of-band changes; fix the template, not just the resource.

gotchas.trap: Running remediation scripts from cron on a single "ops" EC2 instance.
gotchas.correct: Use EventBridge-triggered SSM Automation or Lambda. It is managed, audited and has no single host to fail.

gotchas.trap: Keeping a bastion host with port 22 open to the internet "restricted by keys".
gotchas.correct: Use Session Manager with IAM-controlled access and session logging, and close inbound ports.

gotchas.trap: Fixing drift by editing the resource in the console again.
gotchas.correct: Update the template and redeploy so the IaC stays the source of truth.

lessons.lab: Create an AWS Config managed rule that checks for unrestricted SSH in security groups. Attach a remediation action that uses an AWS-provided Systems Manager Automation runbook, set it to automatic, then open port 22 on a test security group and watch Config remediate it. Separately, connect to a private instance with Session Manager and confirm the session log reaches CloudWatch Logs.

lessons.title: Improving Security Posture and Remediating Findings
lessons.summary: Aggregating findings across an organization, prioritising them, and closing them with automated, auditable remediation.

sections.heading: Detection services and what each finds
sections.body:
- **Amazon GuardDuty**: threat detection from sources such as CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs. Examples include crypto-mining, credential exfiltration and unusual API calls.
- **Amazon Inspector**: software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure on EC2, container images in ECR, and Lambda functions.
- **Amazon Macie**: sensitive data (such as PII) in S3.
- **AWS Config**: configuration compliance against rules and conformance packs.
- **IAM Access Analyzer**: resources shared outside your zone of trust, **unused access** (roles, keys and permissions nobody uses), and policy validation.

sections.heading: Aggregation: Security Hub CSPM and Security Hub
sections.body:
AWS split Security Hub into two services:

- **AWS Security Hub CSPM** is the posture service you may know as "Security Hub". It runs security standards and controls, and it aggregates findings in ASFF.
- The new **AWS Security Hub** (GA December 2025) correlates signals from GuardDuty, Inspector, Security Hub CSPM, Macie and others into **exposures** and risk prioritisation, using OCSF.

In both cases the multi-account pattern is the same. Designate a **delegated administrator** account through AWS Organizations, auto-enable member accounts, and aggregate across Regions. Do not log in to each account to review findings.

sections.heading: Automated remediation
sections.body:
Findings are published to **EventBridge**. Route a specific finding type to a Lambda function, Step Functions workflow or SSM Automation runbook.

Example: GuardDuty reports an EC2 instance communicating with a known crypto-mining pool. The automation:
1. Replaces the instance's security groups with an isolation group that allows no traffic.
2. Snapshots its EBS volumes for investigation.
3. Tags it and notifies the security team.

It does **not** terminate the instance right away, because that destroys evidence. Keep a human approval step for destructive actions.

sections.heading: Common posture improvements
sections.body:
- **Hard-coded or long-lived secrets** → AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation. Applications fetch the secret at runtime.
- **Long-lived IAM user access keys** → IAM roles (for workloads) and IAM Identity Center (for people).
- **Public S3 exposure** → S3 Block Public Access at the account level. Protect the setting with an SCP, and use Access Analyzer to review intended sharing.
- **Unpatched fleets** → Patch Manager with compliance reporting. Inspector shows which CVEs actually affect running resources.
- **Over-broad permissions** → use Access Analyzer unused-access findings and policy generation from CloudTrail activity to shrink policies to what is actually used.
- **Encryption at rest** → KMS customer managed keys with automatic rotation enabled where policy requires.

keyPoints: GuardDuty = threats; Inspector = vulnerabilities; Macie = sensitive data in S3; Config = configuration compliance; Access Analyzer = external and unused access.
Security Hub CSPM (legacy posture service) and the new Security Hub (exposure correlation, GA Dec 2025) are distinct services.
Use a delegated administrator and Organizations auto-enable for org-wide security services.
Remediate through EventBridge-routed automation; isolate and preserve evidence rather than terminating.
Replace embedded credentials with Secrets Manager and rotation; replace IAM user keys with roles.

gotchas.trap: Terminating a compromised instance automatically as soon as GuardDuty fires.
gotchas.correct: Isolate it with a restrictive security group and snapshot volumes so forensics remain possible.

gotchas.trap: Reviewing findings by signing in to each member account.
gotchas.correct: Use a delegated administrator with cross-account and cross-Region aggregation.

gotchas.trap: Calling the legacy posture-checking service simply "Security Hub" in a post-2025 design.
gotchas.correct: Posture checks and standards are in Security Hub CSPM; the new Security Hub correlates findings into exposures.

gotchas.trap: Storing database passwords as encrypted Lambda environment variables and calling it rotated.
gotchas.correct: Store them in Secrets Manager with scheduled rotation and retrieve them at runtime.

Create an EventBridge rule that matches one finding type and invokes a Lambda function that tags the affected resource and posts to an SNS topic. Then turn on IAM Access Analyzer unused-access analysis and review which roles have permissions that were never used.

lessons.title: Improving Performance and Reliability
lessons.summary: Finding the bottleneck or single point of failure in a live system and fixing it with caching, read scaling, decoupling, better scaling policies and tested resilience.

sections.heading: Diagnose before you scale
sections.body:
Pinpoint the constraint first, using metrics, traces and database telemetry. Then choose the fix that removes it:

| Symptom | Typical improvement |
|---|---|
| Read-heavy relational DB at high CPU | Read replicas and/or ElastiCache in front of hot queries |
| Many short-lived Lambda connections exhausting DB connections | **Amazon RDS Proxy** connection pooling |
| DynamoDB read latency must drop to microseconds | **DAX** |
| Global users, slow static/dynamic content | **CloudFront** caching at the edge |
| Spiky write bursts overwhelming a backend | Buffer with **SQS** and process at a controlled rate |

Scaling up the primary instance is rarely the best answer when the load is read-dominated or bursty.

sections.heading: Scaling policies
sections.body:
- **Target tracking** keeps a metric (for example, average CPU or requests per target) near a set value.
- **Predictive scaling** forecasts cyclical patterns and adds capacity *ahead* of them. Use it when instances boot slowly and the load is regular.
- **Scheduled actions** handle known one-off events.
- **Warm pools** keep pre-initialised instances ready to cut scale-out time.

sections.heading: Removing single points of failure
sections.body:
Common findings in existing workloads:

- A single NAT gateway serving private subnets in every AZ. Deploy one NAT gateway **per AZ**, with each AZ's route table pointing to its local gateway.
- A single-AZ database. Enable Multi-AZ.
- Clients retrying in lockstep. Use **exponential backoff with jitter**, timeouts and circuit breakers to avoid retry storms.
- Tight synchronous coupling. Decouple with queues or events so one slow consumer does not take down producers.

sections.heading: Proving resilience
sections.body:
- **AWS Resilience Hub** assesses an application against defined RTO/RPO targets and recommends improvements, and it keeps validating over time.
- **AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS)** runs controlled experiments, such as stopping instances or adding latency, to check that recovery actually works.
- Route 53 health checks and failover routing, along with Amazon Application Recovery Controller, handle traffic shifting. Prefer data-plane mechanisms for failover.

keyPoints: Match the fix to the bottleneck: replicas or caching for reads, RDS Proxy for connection storms, SQS for bursts, CloudFront for distance.
Predictive scaling adds capacity ahead of regular cycles; target tracking reacts to the current load.
One NAT gateway per AZ removes a cross-AZ single point of failure.
Exponential backoff with jitter prevents synchronised retry storms.
Resilience Hub validates RTO/RPO posture; FIS tests it with real faults.

gotchas.trap: Vertically scaling the primary database to fix read contention.
gotchas.correct: Offload reads to replicas and cache hot data. It is cheaper and scales further.

gotchas.trap: Raising the Lambda concurrency limit when the database runs out of connections.
gotchas.correct: Pool connections with RDS Proxy; more concurrency makes connection exhaustion worse.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a DR plan works because it is documented.
gotchas.correct: Test it with FIS experiments and game days, and track posture with Resilience Hub.

lessons.lab: Deploy a small web tier behind an Auto Scaling group with a target tracking policy. Use AWS Fault Injection Service to stop instances in one AZ and observe recovery. Then put an RDS Proxy in front of a test RDS database used by a Lambda function and compare the DatabaseConnections metric under a burst of invocations.

lessons.title: Cost Optimization of Running Workloads
lessons.summary: Right-sizing, commitment discounts, Spot, storage tiering, data-transfer fixes and the visibility tooling that keeps costs from creeping back.

sections.heading: Right-size first, then commit
sections.body:
Buying commitments for an oversized fleet locks in waste. The usual sequence is:

1. **Find idle and oversized resources.** **AWS Compute Optimizer** analyses utilisation and recommends sizes for EC2, Auto Scaling groups, EBS volumes, Lambda functions and more. Install the CloudWatch agent so it can account for memory. Trusted Advisor also flags idle resources.
2. **Turn off what is not needed**, such as non-production environments outside working hours, using scheduled stop/start.
3. **Modernise** where it pays off, for example by moving to Graviton-based instances for better price-performance.
4. **Commit** to the remaining steady baseline.

sections.heading: Purchasing options
sections.body:
| Option | Best for | Flexibility |
|---|---|---|
| **Compute Savings Plans** | Steady compute spend that may change instance family, Region, OS or move between EC2, Fargate and Lambda | Highest |
| **EC2 Instance Savings Plans** | Steady use of one instance family in one Region | Lower flexibility, deeper discount |
| **Reserved Instances** | Specific configurations; RDS and other services with their own RIs | Varies by type |
| **Database Savings Plans** (new Dec 2025) | Steady database spend across supported services such as Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB and ElastiCache | Flexible across engine, instance family and Region |
| **Spot Instances** | Fault-tolerant, interruptible work such as batch, CI and stateless containers | Can be reclaimed with a short notice |
| **On-Demand** | Spiky or unknown usage above the committed baseline | Full |

For Spot, diversify across instance types and AZs and use the **price-capacity-optimized** allocation strategy so fewer interruptions occur.

sections.heading: Storage tiering
sections.body:
- **S3 Intelligent-Tiering** moves objects between access tiers automatically, with no retrieval fees. It is the default when access patterns are unknown or changing.
- **S3 Lifecycle rules** fit *known* patterns (for example, transition to Glacier after 90 days and expire after 7 years). Lifecycle rules can also **abort incomplete multipart uploads**.
- Watch minimum storage durations and per-object transition charges. Moving millions of tiny objects to archive tiers can cost more than it saves.
- **S3 Storage Lens** gives organization-wide visibility into usage and finds optimisation candidates.
- **EBS gp2 → gp3**: gp3 sets IOPS and throughput independently of size and usually costs less. Elastic Volumes changes the type in place without detaching.
- **EFS lifecycle management** moves cold files to cheaper storage classes. **Data Lifecycle Manager** and AWS Backup policies keep snapshot sprawl in check.

sections.heading: Data transfer and network cost
sections.body:
- Traffic from private subnets to S3 or DynamoDB through a **NAT gateway** incurs NAT data-processing charges. A **gateway VPC endpoint** for S3/DynamoDB removes them, because gateway endpoints have no hourly or data-processing charge.
- Keep chatty components in the same AZ where reliability allows, and use CloudFront to reduce origin egress.

sections.heading: Visibility and guardrails
sections.body:
- **Cost allocation tags** must be activated in the Billing console before they appear in cost reports. Enforce tagging with **tag policies**, and group spend by business unit with **cost categories**.
- **Cost Explorer** handles analysis and commitment recommendations. The **Cost and Usage Report / Data Exports**, queried with Athena, provides line-item chargeback.
- **AWS Budgets** sends alerts and can run **budget actions**, such as applying a restrictive policy or stopping instances.
- **Cost Anomaly Detection** uses machine learning to alert on unusual spend without hand-set thresholds.

keyPoints: Right-size and remove idle resources before buying commitments.
Compute Savings Plans: most flexible across family, Region, OS, and EC2/Fargate/Lambda. EC2 Instance Savings Plans: locked to a family and Region for a deeper discount.
Database Savings Plans (Dec 2025) cover steady database spend with engine, family and Region flexibility.
Spot suits interruptible work; diversify types and use price-capacity-optimized allocation.
Intelligent-Tiering for unknown access patterns; Lifecycle rules for known ones.
gp2 → gp3 in place with Elastic Volumes; S3/DynamoDB gateway endpoints remove NAT processing charges.
Tags must be activated; Cost Anomaly Detection catches unexpected spend; Budgets actions can enforce limits.

gotchas.trap: Buying a 3-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan for a fleet that is planned to move to containers on Fargate.
gotchas.correct: Compute Savings Plans also apply to Fargate and Lambda, so they survive the modernisation.

gotchas.trap: Transitioning millions of small objects straight to an archive tier to save money.
gotchas.correct: Check per-object transition charges and minimum durations. Intelligent-Tiering or aggregating objects may be cheaper.

gotchas.trap: Running Spot fleets on a single instance type to keep things simple.
gotchas.correct: Diversify instance types and AZs and use price-capacity-optimized allocation.

gotchas.trap: Expecting newly created tags to appear in Cost Explorer automatically.
gotchas.correct: Activate them as cost allocation tags first.

Add an S3 gateway endpoint to a VPC that reaches S3 through a NAT gateway and compare NAT gateway BytesOutToDestination before and after. Finally, create a Cost Anomaly Detection monitor with an email alert subscription.

lessons.title: Choosing Workloads and Migration Strategies (the 7 Rs)
lessons.summary: How to sort a portfolio into the 7 Rs, decide what to move first, and use discovery and planning tooling, including the 2025-2026 changes to Migration Hub and Application Discovery Service.

sections.heading: The 7 Rs at a glance
sections.body:
AWS Prescriptive Guidance names seven migration strategies. Know each one and a typical example:

| Strategy | What it means | Typical example |
|---|---|---|
| **Retire** | Decommission the application | Zombie or idle servers nobody uses |
| **Retain** | Keep it where it is for now | Recently upgraded, compliance-bound, or not ready to move |
| **Rehost** | Lift and shift, no code changes | VM replicated to EC2 with MGN |
| **Relocate** | Move infrastructure without buying new hardware or rewriting | VMware workloads to VMware Cloud on AWS; moving resources between VPCs, Regions or accounts |
| **Repurchase** | Drop and shop | Replace an on-premises CRM with a SaaS product |
| **Replatform** | Lift, tinker and shift | Self-managed SQL Server to Amazon RDS for SQL Server; containerise with App2Container; move to Graviton |
| **Refactor / re-architect** | Change the architecture to use cloud-native features | Monolith split into containers or serverless services |

Refactor is the most complex and expensive option. For **large migrations**, AWS recommends using rehost, replatform, relocate or retire first and **modernising after** the workload is in AWS.

sections.heading: Finding retire and retain candidates
sections.body:
Discovery data drives the decision more than opinion does:

- **Zombie applications** average under 5% CPU and memory use. They are strong retire candidates.
- **Idle applications** average 5-20% use over a 90-day period. Check them for consolidation or retirement.
- Confirm with the business owner before retiring anything. Low use is a signal, not proof.
- Retain is a valid answer when a deadline, licence, compliance rule or dependency makes moving now a poor choice. It is not a failure.

sections.heading: Discovery and planning tools: what changed
sections.body:
The SAP-C02 exam guide still lists **AWS Migration Hub** and **AWS Application Discovery Service**. Their status has changed:

- **AWS Migration Hub** closed to new customers on 2025-11-07. Existing customers keep access but get no new features.
- **AWS Application Discovery Service** closed to new customers on the same date and is in maintenance.
- **AWS Transform** (launched May 2025) is the recommended replacement for discovery, assessment and wave planning.

For exam scenarios, the concepts stay the same: collect inventory, utilisation and dependency data; group servers that talk to each other into the same **wave**; then track progress centrally. In a real 2026 project for a new AWS customer, start with AWS Transform.

sections.heading: Wave planning
sections.body:
- Group servers by **application and dependency**, not by data centre rack. Moving half of a chatty application adds latency across the hybrid link.
- Start with a few low-risk pilot waves to prove the process, then scale out with a repeatable factory approach (for example Cloud Migration Factory).
- Set business-driven deadlines (data centre exit, contract end) first, then pick the fastest strategy that meets them for each app.

keyPoints: Know all seven Rs and a concrete example of each; Relocate and Repurchase are the most often confused.
For large, deadline-driven migrations, migrate first (rehost/replatform/relocate/retire) and modernise afterwards.
Refactor gives the most cloud benefit but costs the most time and money.
Zombie (<5% use) and idle (5-20% over 90 days) apps are retire candidates once owners confirm.
Migration Hub and Application Discovery Service closed to new customers on 2025-11-07; AWS Transform replaces them.
Wave plans group servers by application dependency.

gotchas.trap: Refactor every application to microservices before moving so you only migrate once.
gotchas.correct: At scale this misses deadlines. AWS guidance is to migrate quickly with rehost/replatform and modernise after migration.

gotchas.trap: Relocate means moving VMs to EC2 instances.
gotchas.correct: Moving VMs to EC2 unchanged is Rehost. Relocate is, for example, moving VMware workloads to VMware Cloud on AWS, or moving resources between VPCs, Regions or accounts.

gotchas.trap: A new customer should start discovery with Application Discovery Service.
gotchas.correct: It is closed to new customers. AWS recommends AWS Transform for discovery and assessment.

lessons.lab: Take a list of 20 fictional applications with utilisation, licence and dependency notes. Assign each one an R, explain why in one sentence, and group the moving ones into three waves so no wave splits a dependency.
