lessons.title: Server and Database Migration Tooling: MGN, DMS and Schema Conversion
lessons.summary: Rehosting servers with Application Migration Service (now AWS Transform MGN) and moving databases with AWS DMS, DMS Schema Conversion and AWS SCT.

sections.heading: Rehosting servers with MGN
sections.body:
**AWS Application Migration Service (MGN, renamed AWS Transform MGN in June 2026)** is the primary AWS rehost tool. It is also the replication engine behind AWS Transform.

- An agent on each source server (physical, virtual or another cloud) performs **continuous block-level replication** into a lightweight **staging area** in your AWS account.
- You launch **test instances** at any time without stopping replication, then launch **cutover instances** when ready. Downtime is limited to the final cutover window.
- Replication traffic can use **private IP addresses** over AWS Direct Connect or VPN instead of the public internet.
- After you validate the cutover instance, **finalise the cutover** so replication resources are cleaned up.

**VM Import/Export** also rehosts, but it imports an image snapshot. It has no continuous replication, so it fits small numbers of VMs that can tolerate downtime.

sections.heading: Moving databases with AWS DMS
sections.body:
**AWS Database Migration Service (DMS)** moves data between engines or within the same engine.

- **Full load** copies existing data. **Change data capture (CDC)** then applies ongoing changes so the source stays live until cutover.
- **Homogeneous** migrations (for example MySQL to Aurora MySQL) need no schema conversion.
- **Heterogeneous** migrations (for example Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL) need the schema and code objects converted first. DMS moves **data**, not stored procedures or schema logic.

sections.heading: Converting schemas: DMS Schema Conversion and SCT
sections.body:
- **DMS Schema Conversion** is a managed, web-based feature of DMS built on the **AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT)** engine. It converts schemas and code, **not data**.
- Generative-AI-assisted conversion is available for some sources (such as Oracle, SQL Server, Db2 and SAP ASE) to PostgreSQL targets.
- SCT is still a desktop tool and remains in scope. Both produce an assessment report showing which objects need manual work.

Typical heterogeneous flow: assess and convert schema, apply it to the target, run DMS full load plus CDC, test, then cut over when replication lag is small.

sections.heading: Matching tool to tier
sections.body:
In a three-tier application you usually mix tools:

- Web and app servers: rehost with MGN.
- Database changing engine: DMS Schema Conversion or SCT plus DMS.
- Database keeping the same engine but moving to a managed service: DMS (or native engine tools), which is a replatform.

Do not rehost a database server with MGN when the requirement is to change engines or move to a managed service.

keyPoints: MGN (AWS Transform MGN) = continuous block-level replication, non-disruptive test launches, short cutover.
VM Import/Export imports images once; no continuous replication.
DMS full load + CDC keeps the source live until cutover.
DMS moves data; DMS Schema Conversion and SCT convert schema and code.
Heterogeneous = convert schema first; homogeneous = data only.
MGN replication can use private IPs over Direct Connect or VPN.

gotchas.trap: DMS alone converts Oracle PL/SQL procedures to PostgreSQL.
gotchas.correct: DMS moves data. Use DMS Schema Conversion or AWS SCT for schema and code objects.

gotchas.trap: Use VM Import/Export for hundreds of servers that need minimal downtime.
gotchas.correct: Use MGN. It replicates continuously and cuts over in minutes.

gotchas.trap: Application Migration Service no longer exists.
gotchas.correct: It was renamed AWS Transform MGN in June 2026. The SAP-C02 guide uses the older name.

lessons.lab: Draw the cutover runbook for a three-tier app: MGN for two app servers, DMS Schema Conversion plus DMS full load and CDC for an Oracle database moving to Aurora PostgreSQL. Mark the point where writes stop and where DNS changes.

lessons.title: Moving Data: DataSync, Transfer Family, Transfer Acceleration and Offline Options
lessons.summary: Online and offline data transfer choices, and why Snow Family devices are no longer the default answer for new customers.

sections.heading: AWS DataSync for bulk online transfer
sections.body:
**AWS DataSync** moves file and object data online between on-premises storage (NFS, SMB, HDFS, object stores), other clouds and AWS storage (Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx).

- An **agent** runs near the source storage.
- Tasks can be scheduled for **incremental** runs, so you sync repeatedly and do a short final pass at cutover.
- It verifies data integrity and can throttle bandwidth so production traffic is not starved.
- It runs over the internet, VPN or Direct Connect.

It is the default answer when the network can carry the data in the time allowed.

sections.heading: AWS Transfer Family for partner file exchange
sections.body:
**AWS Transfer Family** gives a managed **SFTP, FTPS, FTP or AS2** endpoint that stores files in Amazon S3 or Amazon EFS.

- External partners keep their existing clients and workflows.
- You can keep the same hostname by pointing DNS at the new endpoint.
- It replaces a self-managed SFTP server; it is not a bulk migration tool.

sections.heading: S3 Transfer Acceleration
sections.body: **S3 Transfer Acceleration** speeds up long-distance uploads to a single bucket by routing them through AWS edge locations. Use it when clients are far from the bucket Region. It is a per-bucket setting and uses a different endpoint name; it does not copy data between Regions.

sections.heading: Offline transfer in 2026
sections.body:
The SAP-C02 guide still lists the **Snow Family**, but:

- **Snowball Edge** closed to new customers on 2025-11-07.
- **Snowcone** and **Snowmobile** are discontinued.
- New customers should use **DataSync** online, **AWS Data Transfer Terminal** (bring your own storage devices to an AWS facility and upload to S3 or EFS), or AWS partners. Use **AWS Outposts** for edge compute.

A quick test: if data size divided by usable bandwidth fits the deadline, transfer online. If not, plan a physical transfer and still use DataSync for the changes made after the bulk copy.

keyPoints: DataSync = agent-based, scheduled, incremental, integrity-checked online transfer to S3/EFS/FSx.
Transfer Family = managed SFTP/FTPS/FTP/AS2 into S3 or EFS for partner exchange.
S3 Transfer Acceleration = faster long-distance uploads to one bucket through edge locations.
Snowball Edge closed to new customers (2025-11-07); Snowcone and Snowmobile are discontinued.
AWS Data Transfer Terminal is the physical option for new customers.
Do the bandwidth arithmetic before choosing online or offline.

gotchas.trap: Order Snowball Edge devices for a first-time AWS customer.
gotchas.correct: New customers cannot order Snowball Edge. Use DataSync, Data Transfer Terminal or a partner.

gotchas.trap: Use DataSync so partners can keep sending files over SFTP.
gotchas.correct: DataSync is for bulk transfers you run. Transfer Family provides a managed SFTP endpoint for partners.

gotchas.trap: S3 Transfer Acceleration replicates data between Regions.
gotchas.correct: It only speeds uploads and downloads to one bucket. Use S3 Replication to copy between buckets.

lessons.lab: For three cases (50 TB over 1 Gbps in 30 days; 1.5 PB over 500 Mbps in 60 days; daily partner SFTP drops), calculate rough transfer time and pick a service, noting anything that changed for new customers.

lessons.title: Modernisation Architectures: Containers, Serverless, Purpose-Built Databases and Decoupling
lessons.summary: Target architectures after migration: containers and Fargate, Lambda and event-driven design, purpose-built databases, and decoupling with SQS, SNS and EventBridge, plus the strangler fig pattern.

sections.heading: Incremental modernisation with the strangler fig
sections.body: Rewriting a monolith in one go is risky. The **strangler fig** pattern puts a routing layer (for example an Application Load Balancer or Amazon API Gateway) in front of the monolith. New or rewritten features are routed to new services one path at a time, and the monolith shrinks until it can be retired. Each new service should own its data instead of sharing the monolith database.

sections.heading: Containers
sections.body:
- **Amazon ECS** and **Amazon EKS** run containers; choose EKS when the team already uses Kubernetes tooling.
- **AWS Fargate** removes the need to manage EC2 hosts for either orchestrator.
- **AWS App2Container** analyses existing Java and .NET applications and generates container images and deployment artefacts, a replatform step with no code rewrite.
- Containers suit long-running processes, steady traffic and jobs longer than the Lambda timeout.

sections.heading: Serverless and event-driven
sections.body:
- **AWS Lambda** suits short, event-triggered work. A single invocation is capped at 15 minutes; move longer jobs to Fargate tasks or split them into steps. Lambda durable functions (launched December 2025) checkpoint multi-step workflows, but each invocation is still limited to 15 minutes.
- **AWS Step Functions** orchestrates multi-step workflows with retries and error handling.
- Event sources include S3 event notifications, SQS queues, EventBridge rules and schedules, and API Gateway.

sections.heading: Decoupling: SQS, SNS and EventBridge
sections.body:
| Service | Model | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| **Amazon SQS** | Queue, consumers poll | Buffer bursts; protect a slow downstream; scale workers on queue depth. **FIFO** queues keep order per message group. |
| **Amazon SNS** | Pub/sub push | Fan out one message to many subscribers; SNS to multiple SQS queues gives each consumer its own buffer. |
| **Amazon EventBridge** | Event bus with rules | Content-based routing to many targets, events from SaaS partners and AWS services, schedules, archive and replay. |

A single SQS queue shared by several services delivers each message to **only one** consumer; it is not fan-out.

sections.heading: Purpose-built databases
sections.body:
Move away from one-size-fits-all relational databases where access patterns call for it:

- **Amazon DynamoDB**: key-value and document access at any scale with single-digit millisecond latency; on-demand capacity for unpredictable traffic.
- **Amazon Aurora / RDS**: relational with joins and transactions.
- **Amazon Neptune**: highly connected graph data (fraud rings, recommendations).
- **Amazon ElastiCache**: in-memory caching and sessions.
- **Amazon Redshift**: analytical data warehouse queries.
- **Amazon OpenSearch Service**: full-text search and log analytics.

keyPoints: Strangler fig = route features one by one from the monolith to new services.
Fargate removes host management for ECS and EKS; App2Container containerises Java/.NET apps without rewriting.
Lambda max run time is 15 minutes; longer jobs go to Fargate or Step Functions.
SQS buffers; SNS fans out; EventBridge routes by content and integrates SaaS sources.
SQS FIFO with a message group ID keeps per-entity ordering.
Pick the database by access pattern: key-value, relational, graph, cache, warehouse, search.

gotchas.trap: Several services can share one SQS queue to each receive every order event.
gotchas.correct: Each message goes to one consumer. Use SNS-to-SQS fan-out or EventBridge rules to separate queues.

gotchas.trap: Raise the Lambda timeout to run a 45-minute job.
gotchas.correct: Lambda caps at 15 minutes. Use an ECS task on Fargate or break the work into Step Functions steps.

gotchas.trap: New microservices should keep reading and writing the monolith database.
gotchas.correct: Shared databases keep services coupled. Give each service its own data store and sync through events.

lessons.lab: Redesign a synchronous order flow (order -> inventory -> billing -> email) into an event-driven design. Mark which hops use SQS, SNS or EventBridge and why, and note where a FIFO queue is required.

flashcards.front: Is VPC peering transitive?
flashcards.back: No. If A peers with B and B peers with C, A cannot reach C through B. Use Transit Gateway or a direct A-C peering link.

flashcards.front: What is AWS Transit Gateway?
flashcards.back: A Regional layer-3 virtual router. It connects VPCs, Site-to-Site VPNs, Direct Connect gateways, TGW Connect (SD-WAN) and peered transit gateways, with route tables for segmentation.

flashcards.front: Which routing does inter-Region Transit Gateway peering support?
flashcards.back: Static routes only. Propagation and ECMP are not supported over TGW peering.

flashcards.front: What does Transit Gateway appliance mode do?
flashcards.back: It keeps both directions of a flow on the same AZ in an inspection VPC, so stateful firewalls do not see asymmetric traffic.

flashcards.front: On a Transit Gateway, which wins for the same prefix: a Direct Connect gateway route or a VPN route?
flashcards.back: The Direct Connect route. The VPN route acts as the backup.

flashcards.front: What does the Direct Connect maximum resiliency model look like?
flashcards.back: Separate connections on separate devices in more than one DX location. It carries a 99.99% SLA.

flashcards.front: What does the Direct Connect development and test model look like?
flashcards.back: Separate devices in a single location. It offers no protection if that location fails.

flashcards.front: What does a Route 53 VPC Resolver inbound endpoint do?
flashcards.back: It lets on-premises DNS servers forward queries into a VPC to resolve AWS names, such as private hosted zones.

flashcards.front: What does a Route 53 VPC Resolver outbound endpoint do?
flashcards.back: Together with forwarding rules, it lets VPC workloads resolve on-premises domains by forwarding queries to on-premises DNS servers.

flashcards.front: How do you reuse one set of Resolver forwarding rules in many accounts?
flashcards.back: Share the rules with AWS RAM and associate them with VPCs in the consuming accounts.

flashcards.front: When is AWS PrivateLink the best fit?
flashcards.back: When you publish one service (behind an NLB) to many consumer VPCs or accounts, especially with overlapping CIDRs, and do not want full network routing between them.

flashcards.front: What does an SCP do?
flashcards.back: It sets the maximum permissions for principals in member accounts. It never grants permissions and does not affect the management account.

flashcards.front: What does an RCP do?
flashcards.back: It sets the maximum permissions on resources in member accounts, including requests from principals outside the organization. It is a data-perimeter control.

flashcards.front: Name three things RCPs do NOT affect.
flashcards.back: The management account, service-linked roles and AWS managed KMS keys.

flashcards.front: Which Organizations feature set do RCPs require?
flashcards.back: All features. They are not available in consolidated-billing-only organizations.

flashcards.front: What is a permissions boundary?
flashcards.back: A managed policy that caps the maximum permissions an IAM user or role can have. It is used to let teams create roles safely.

flashcards.front: What is an IAM Identity Center permission set?
flashcards.back: A template of permissions that Identity Center provisions as an IAM role in each account it is assigned to.

flashcards.front: What two things are needed for account B to use a KMS key in account A?
flashcards.back: The key policy in A must allow account B (or a principal in it), and an IAM policy in B must allow the KMS actions on that key.

flashcards.front: Why can't you share a secret encrypted with aws/secretsmanager across accounts?
flashcards.back: AWS managed keys cannot be used cross-account. Encrypt the secret with a customer managed key whose policy allows the consumer.

flashcards.front: What is AWS Security Hub CSPM?
flashcards.back: The posture-management service previously called Security Hub. It runs standards checks and aggregates ASFF findings. The newer AWS Security Hub correlates findings into prioritized exposures.

flashcards.front: How should GuardDuty be deployed across an organization?
flashcards.back: Designate a delegated administrator (a security account) and turn on auto-enable so all existing and new member accounts are covered.

flashcards.front: Define RTO and RPO.
flashcards.back: RTO is the maximum acceptable downtime. RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time.

flashcards.front: Pilot light versus warm standby?
flashcards.back: Pilot light keeps data live but the app tier off, so it cannot serve traffic until you act. Warm standby runs a scaled-down, fully working stack that can serve traffic right away.

flashcards.front: Does AWS Backup restore automatically in the DR Region?
flashcards.back: No. It copies backups across Regions and accounts but has no scheduled or automatic restore. You automate restore yourself.

flashcards.front: Aurora Global Database switchover versus failover?
flashcards.back: Switchover is for planned or healthy events and gives RPO 0. Failover (allow data loss) is for unplanned outages and has a non-zero RPO.

flashcards.front: Which failover mechanisms are data-plane operations?
flashcards.back: Route 53 health checks with failover records, and Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) routing controls.

flashcards.front: Which workloads does Elastic Disaster Recovery protect on AWS?
flashcards.back: EC2 instances, using block-level replication. It does not protect RDS. Use database-native replication or backups for RDS.

flashcards.front: What are the three kinds of AWS Control Tower controls?
flashcards.back: Preventive (block actions), detective (find noncompliance with Config), and proactive (check resources before provisioning with CloudFormation hooks).

flashcards.front: What must you do before a resource tag appears in Cost Explorer?
flashcards.back: Activate it as a cost allocation tag in the management (payer) account. By default it applies only from activation onward.

flashcards.front: How do you allocate a shared networking account's cost to business units?
flashcards.back: Use AWS Cost Categories with split charge rules to distribute the shared cost across consuming categories.

flashcards.front: Are RI and Savings Plans discounts shared across an organization?
flashcards.back: Yes, by default under consolidated billing. The management account can turn sharing off for specific accounts.

flashcards.front: What does `cdk synth` produce?
flashcards.back: CloudFormation templates. The CDK deploys through CloudFormation.

flashcards.front: CloudFormation change set vs drift detection?
flashcards.back: A change set previews what an update will add, modify or replace. Drift detection finds changes made to live resources outside CloudFormation.

flashcards.front: What do CloudFormation StackSets do?
flashcards.back: Deploy one template to many accounts and Regions in one operation. With service-managed permissions they can auto-deploy to new accounts in a target OU.

flashcards.front: DeletionPolicy vs UpdateReplacePolicy?
flashcards.back: DeletionPolicy applies when the resource is removed or the stack is deleted. UpdateReplacePolicy applies to the old resource when an update forces replacement. Both accept Retain, Snapshot (where supported) or Delete.

flashcards.front: What are CloudFormation rollback triggers?
flashcards.back: CloudWatch alarms that CloudFormation monitors during a create or update. If one fires, the operation rolls back.

flashcards.front: How do you pass a database password into CloudFormation safely?
flashcards.back: Use a dynamic reference such as `{{resolve:secretsmanager:...}}`, or let RDS manage the master password in Secrets Manager. Do not put it in parameters or the template.

flashcards.front: CloudFormation Hooks vs AWS Config rules?
flashcards.back: Hooks evaluate resources before provisioning and can block them (proactive). Config rules evaluate resources after they exist (detective).

flashcards.front: What is a CDK Aspect?
flashcards.back: A visitor applied to every construct in a scope, used to check or change configuration (for example, enforce bucket encryption) across a CDK app.

flashcards.front: Key requirement for a cross-account CodePipeline artifact bucket?
flashcards.back: Encrypt it with a customer managed KMS key whose key policy grants the target accounts' roles. AWS managed keys cannot be shared cross-account.

flashcards.front: Canary vs linear deployment?
flashcards.back: Canary shifts a small percentage first, then the rest after a wait. Linear shifts equal increments at fixed intervals until 100%.

flashcards.front: How does CodeDeploy do Lambda deployments?
flashcards.back: It shifts traffic on an alias between two versions (canary, linear or all-at-once) and rolls back automatically if a configured CloudWatch alarm fires.

flashcards.front: What does the ECS test listener in a CodeDeploy blue/green deployment do?
flashcards.back: Sends test traffic to the green task set so you can validate it before production traffic is shifted.

flashcards.front: What is the ECS deployment circuit breaker?
flashcards.back: It detects a rolling deployment that cannot reach a steady state and can roll back to the last completed deployment automatically.

flashcards.front: Pilot light vs warm standby?
flashcards.back: Pilot light keeps data replicating but the app tier is off, so it cannot serve traffic without action. Warm standby is a scaled-down working copy that can take traffic immediately.

flashcards.front: Which DR strategy has the lowest cost and highest RTO?
flashcards.back: Backup and restore: redeploy infrastructure with IaC and restore data from backups.

flashcards.front: Aurora Global Database switchover vs failover?
flashcards.back: Switchover (formerly managed planned failover) is for planned or healthy cases with RPO 0. Failover is for unplanned outages and can lose recent writes.

flashcards.front: How many secondary Regions can an Aurora Global Database have?
flashcards.back: Up to five, with typical replication lag under one second.

flashcards.front: Why fail over with data-plane operations?
flashcards.back: Control planes are more likely to be impaired during an event. Route 53 health checks and ARC routing controls work on the data plane.

flashcards.front: What is static stability?
flashcards.back: Running enough pre-provisioned capacity that the system keeps working after an AZ (or Region) loss without launching new resources.

flashcards.front: Can AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery protect Amazon RDS?
flashcards.back: No. For AWS-hosted sources it replicates EC2 instances. Use database-native replication or AWS Backup for RDS.

flashcards.front: How do you health check a private resource with Route 53?
flashcards.back: Create a CloudWatch alarm on a metric for the resource and base the Route 53 health check on the alarm.

flashcards.front: Route 53 latency vs geolocation routing?
flashcards.back: Latency routes to the Region with the lowest latency for the user. Geolocation routes by the user's location, which suits residency or localization rules.

flashcards.front: When choose Global Accelerator over CloudFront?
flashcards.back: For non-HTTP (TCP/UDP) traffic or when you need static anycast IPs and fast failover that does not depend on DNS caching.

flashcards.front: Why must SQS standard queue consumers be idempotent?
flashcards.back: Standard queues deliver at least once, so the same message can arrive more than once.

flashcards.front: Step Functions Standard vs Express?
flashcards.back: Standard: long-running (up to a year), exactly-once, suits human approvals. Express: high-volume, short (up to five minutes), at-least-once.

flashcards.front: Security group vs network ACL?
flashcards.back: Security groups are stateful, attach to ENIs and only allow. NACLs are stateless, apply to subnets, support allow and deny, and need return-traffic rules.

flashcards.front: Gateway vs interface VPC endpoint?
flashcards.back: Gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB) use route-table entries and have no charge. Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) put ENIs in subnets for many services and are billed.

flashcards.front: Shield Standard vs Shield Advanced?
flashcards.back: Standard is automatic and free. Advanced adds DDoS response team support, enhanced detection and cost protection for attack-driven scaling.

flashcards.front: How do you restrict an S3 origin to CloudFront?
flashcards.back: Use origin access control (OAC) and a bucket policy that allows only the CloudFront service principal for that distribution. Keep Block Public Access on.

flashcards.front: In which Region must an ACM certificate for CloudFront be?
flashcards.back: us-east-1 (N. Virginia).

flashcards.front: Cognito user pool vs identity pool?
flashcards.back: A user pool authenticates users and issues JWTs. An identity pool exchanges identities for temporary AWS credentials via IAM roles.

flashcards.front: Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store SecureString?
flashcards.back: Secrets Manager has built-in rotation (managed or via Lambda). Parameter Store SecureString stores encrypted values but has no built-in rotation.

flashcards.front: What problem does RDS Proxy solve?
flashcards.back: Connection storms and exhaustion, for example from many concurrent Lambda functions. It pools and reuses database connections.

flashcards.front: What is DAX?
flashcards.back: An in-memory cache for DynamoDB with microsecond read latency through a DynamoDB-compatible API.

flashcards.front: Compute Savings Plans vs EC2 Instance Savings Plans?
flashcards.back: Compute SPs apply across instance families, Regions, Fargate and Lambda. EC2 Instance SPs are tied to a family in a Region but give a deeper discount.

flashcards.front: What are Database Savings Plans?
flashcards.back: A commitment discount (launched December 2025) for steady database spend across services such as Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB and ElastiCache, flexible across engine, family and Region.

flashcards.front: EFS vs FSx for Lustre vs FSx for Windows?
flashcards.back: EFS: shared NFS for Linux across AZs. FSx for Lustre: high-throughput HPC storage that can link to S3. FSx for Windows: SMB with Active Directory.

flashcards.front: Why is gp3 often a better default than gp2?
flashcards.back: gp3 lets you provision IOPS and throughput independently of volume size, usually at a lower cost per GiB.

flashcards.front: What does a CloudWatch metric filter do?
flashcards.back: It turns matching log events in a log group into a CloudWatch metric, which you can then graph and alarm on.

flashcards.front: Why can't Compute Optimizer or CloudWatch see EC2 memory utilisation by default?
flashcards.back: Memory is an OS-level metric. Install the CloudWatch agent to publish it.

flashcards.front: Composite alarm
flashcards.back: A CloudWatch alarm whose state comes from other alarms combined with AND/OR/NOT logic. It is used to reduce alert noise.

flashcards.front: CloudWatch Synthetics canary
flashcards.back: A scheduled script that probes endpoints or user journeys from outside, so failures are detected before users report them.

flashcards.front: X-Ray / ADOT tracing: when?
flashcards.back: When latency or errors are spread across several services and you need to find the hop responsible.

flashcards.front: CloudWatch cross-account observability
flashcards.back: Links source accounts to a central monitoring account, so you can see metrics, logs and traces across accounts without switching.

flashcards.front: How do you centralise log storage from many accounts?
flashcards.back: Use CloudWatch Logs subscription filters to stream to a central destination (for example, Firehose to S3 in a log-archive account).

flashcards.front: Session Manager benefits
flashcards.back: No inbound ports, bastion or SSH keys. Access is controlled by IAM and sessions can be logged to S3 or CloudWatch Logs.

flashcards.front: Default pattern to automate a manual runbook
flashcards.back: An EventBridge rule or CloudWatch alarm triggers a Systems Manager Automation runbook (or Lambda / Step Functions).

flashcards.front: AWS Config remediation
flashcards.back: A non-compliant rule evaluation triggers an SSM Automation document, either manually or automatically.

flashcards.front: Patch Manager core concepts
flashcards.back: Patch baselines define approved patches, maintenance windows control timing, and compliance is reported per instance.

flashcards.front: CloudFormation drift detection
flashcards.back: Finds resources changed outside the stack. Fix by updating the template, not by re-editing the resource.

flashcards.front: GuardDuty vs Inspector vs Macie
flashcards.back: GuardDuty = threat detection; Inspector = software vulnerabilities and exposure (EC2, ECR, Lambda); Macie = sensitive data in S3.

flashcards.front: Security Hub CSPM vs new Security Hub
flashcards.back: Security Hub CSPM is the legacy posture/standards service (ASFF). The new Security Hub (GA Dec 2025) correlates findings into exposures using OCSF.

flashcards.front: How do you run a security service across an organization?
flashcards.back: Designate a delegated administrator account through AWS Organizations, auto-enable member accounts, and aggregate Regions.

flashcards.front: First automated response to a compromised EC2 instance
flashcards.back: Isolate it with a no-traffic security group and snapshot its volumes. Do not terminate it, so evidence is preserved.

flashcards.front: IAM Access Analyzer unused access
flashcards.back: Reports roles, access keys and permissions that are granted but not used, which helps you move toward least privilege.

flashcards.front: Fix for database passwords in code or environment variables
flashcards.back: AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation; the application retrieves the secret at runtime.

flashcards.front: Lambda exhausting relational DB connections
flashcards.back: Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the database to pool and reuse connections.

flashcards.front: Predictive scaling vs target tracking
flashcards.back: Predictive forecasts regular cycles and adds capacity ahead of them. Target tracking reacts to keep a metric near a target.

flashcards.front: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
flashcards.back: It spreads retries out in time, so many clients do not retry in lockstep and overload a recovering service.

flashcards.front: AWS Resilience Hub vs Fault Injection Service
flashcards.back: Resilience Hub assesses and tracks whether an app meets its RTO/RPO. FIS injects real faults to test that recovery works.

flashcards.front: Compute Savings Plans flexibility
flashcards.back: Applies across instance family, size, Region, OS and tenancy, and also covers Fargate and Lambda.

flashcards.front: EC2 Instance Savings Plans
flashcards.back: Commit to one instance family in one Region for a deeper discount than Compute Savings Plans, with less flexibility.

flashcards.front: Database Savings Plans
flashcards.back: Commitment pricing launched Dec 2025 for database services such as Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB and ElastiCache. Flexible across engine, instance family and Region.

flashcards.front: Spot best practices
flashcards.back: Use for interruptible work, diversify instance types and AZs, and use the price-capacity-optimized allocation strategy.

flashcards.front: S3 Intelligent-Tiering vs Lifecycle rules
flashcards.back: Intelligent-Tiering suits unknown or changing access (automatic, no retrieval fees). Lifecycle rules suit known, age-based patterns.

flashcards.front: gp2 → gp3 migration
flashcards.back: Change the volume type in place with Elastic Volumes. gp3 sets IOPS and throughput independently of size and is usually cheaper.

flashcards.front: Cutting NAT gateway charges for S3 traffic
flashcards.back: Add an S3 gateway VPC endpoint. Gateway endpoints have no hourly or data-processing charge.

flashcards.front: Cost allocation tags gotcha
flashcards.back: User-defined tags must be activated as cost allocation tags in Billing before they appear in Cost Explorer or cost reports.

flashcards.front: Cost Anomaly Detection
flashcards.back: Machine-learning monitors that alert on unusual spend without hand-set thresholds.

flashcards.front: AWS Budgets actions
flashcards.back: When a budget threshold is crossed, Budgets can automatically apply an IAM policy or SCP, or stop EC2/RDS instances.

flashcards.front: Name the 7 Rs of migration.
flashcards.back: Retire, Retain, Rehost, Relocate, Repurchase, Replatform, Refactor (re-architect).

flashcards.front: Rehost vs Replatform?
flashcards.back: Rehost = lift and shift with no changes (e.g., VM to EC2 with MGN). Replatform = lift, tinker and shift with small optimisations (e.g., SQL Server to Amazon RDS for SQL Server).

flashcards.front: What is the Relocate strategy?
flashcards.back: Moving infrastructure without new hardware, rewriting or changing operations, e.g., VMware workloads to VMware Cloud on AWS, or moving resources between VPCs, Regions or accounts.

flashcards.front: What is Repurchase ("drop and shop")?
flashcards.back: Replacing an application with a different product, usually SaaS, e.g., a self-hosted CRM replaced by a SaaS CRM.

flashcards.front: For a large, deadline-driven migration, when does AWS recommend modernising?
flashcards.back: After migration. Move first with rehost, replatform, relocate or retire, then modernise in AWS.

flashcards.front: Which apps are retire candidates by utilisation?
flashcards.back: Zombie apps (under 5% average CPU and memory) and idle apps (5-20% over 90 days), after the business owner confirms.

flashcards.front: Status of AWS Migration Hub and Application Discovery Service?
flashcards.back: Both closed to new customers on 2025-11-07. Existing customers keep access. AWS Transform is the recommended replacement for discovery, assessment and planning.

flashcards.front: What does Application Migration Service (MGN) do, and what is it called now?
flashcards.back: Continuous block-level replication of physical, virtual or cloud servers into a staging area, then test and cutover launches on EC2. Renamed AWS Transform MGN in June 2026.

flashcards.front: MGN vs VM Import/Export?
flashcards.back: MGN replicates continuously and cuts over with minimal downtime at scale. VM Import/Export imports a one-time image with no ongoing replication.

flashcards.front: How do you keep MGN replication off the public internet?
flashcards.back: Configure replication to use private IP addresses and route it over Direct Connect or VPN to the staging area subnet.

flashcards.front: What do DMS full load and CDC do?
flashcards.back: Full load copies existing data; change data capture applies ongoing source changes so the source stays live until a short cutover.

flashcards.front: What does DMS Schema Conversion (or AWS SCT) do that DMS replication does not?
flashcards.back: Converts schema and code objects (tables, views, procedures) between engines. It does not move data. DMS Schema Conversion is the managed web-based version built on the SCT engine.

flashcards.front: Homogeneous vs heterogeneous database migration?
flashcards.back: Homogeneous = same engine (e.g., MySQL to Aurora MySQL), data only. Heterogeneous = different engine (e.g., Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL), so convert schema and code first.

flashcards.front: When is AWS DataSync the right tool?
flashcards.back: Online bulk or recurring transfer of file and object data (NFS, SMB, HDFS, object) into S3, EFS or FSx, with scheduling, incremental runs, integrity checks and bandwidth throttling.

flashcards.front: When is AWS Transfer Family the right tool?
flashcards.back: When partners or systems exchange files over SFTP, FTPS, FTP or AS2 and you want a managed endpoint that stores into S3 or EFS without changing their clients.

flashcards.front: What does S3 Transfer Acceleration do?
flashcards.back: Speeds long-distance uploads and downloads to one S3 bucket by routing traffic through AWS edge locations. It does not replicate data between Regions.

flashcards.front: Snow Family status for new customers (2026)?
flashcards.back: Snowball Edge closed to new customers on 2025-11-07; Snowcone and Snowmobile are discontinued. Use DataSync, AWS Data Transfer Terminal or partners; use Outposts for edge compute.

flashcards.front: What is AWS Data Transfer Terminal?
flashcards.back: A physical transfer option: you bring your own storage devices to an AWS facility and upload the data to Amazon S3 or Amazon EFS.

flashcards.front: What is the strangler fig pattern?
flashcards.back: Put a router (ALB or API Gateway) in front of a monolith and move features to new services one route at a time until the monolith can be retired.

flashcards.front: SQS vs SNS vs EventBridge in one line each?
flashcards.back: SQS = durable queue that buffers work for polling consumers. SNS = push pub/sub fan-out. EventBridge = event bus with content-based rules, SaaS and AWS sources, schedules, archive and replay.

flashcards.front: How do you keep strict per-customer ordering in a queue?
flashcards.back: Use an SQS FIFO queue with the customer ID as the message group ID.

flashcards.front: A batch job runs 45 minutes. Lambda or Fargate?
flashcards.back: Fargate (for example an ECS task started by EventBridge). A Lambda invocation is capped at 15 minutes.

flashcards.front: What does AWS App2Container do?
flashcards.back: Analyses existing Java and .NET applications and generates container images and ECS or EKS deployment artefacts, a replatform without code changes.

flashcards.front: Match: graph relationships, key-value at massive scale, analytics warehouse.
flashcards.back: Amazon Neptune; Amazon DynamoDB; Amazon Redshift.

questions.stem:
A company has 150 VPCs across 40 accounts in one Region and two data centers connected with Direct Connect. Today each VPC peers with several others, and the network team cannot keep up with route and peering changes. Production VPCs must not be able to reach development VPCs.

Which design reduces operational overhead while meeting the segmentation requirement?
options: Create a full mesh of VPC peering connections, automated with CloudFormation StackSets.
Expose every VPC's services through AWS PrivateLink endpoint services and remove all routing between VPCs.
Create a transit VPC with peering to every spoke VPC and route spoke-to-spoke traffic through it.
Deploy a Transit Gateway shared through AWS RAM, attach every VPC and a Direct Connect gateway, and use separate TGW route tables for prod and non-prod.
questions.explanation: Transit Gateway is the managed hub for many VPCs plus hybrid connectivity, and its route tables give segmentation. Sharing it through RAM lets every account attach to it. Peering does not scale and is non-transitive.
rationales: A full mesh still grows as n(n-1)/2 connections. Automating it does not remove the route-table sprawl.
PrivateLink publishes individual services. It does not give general bidirectional connectivity or on-premises routing.
Peering is non-transitive, so traffic cannot pass through a hub VPC this way.
Correct. One TGW handles VPCs and DX, and separate route tables isolate prod from non-prod.

questions.stem:
A security team routes all east-west traffic between spoke VPCs through a Transit Gateway to an inspection VPC that runs stateful firewalls in two Availability Zones. Some connections between spokes in different AZs fail at random, and the firewall logs show sessions with no matching SYN.

What is the most likely fix?
options: Enable appliance mode on the inspection VPC's Transit Gateway attachment.
Enable ECMP on the Transit Gateway.
Replace the Transit Gateway with VPC peering between each spoke and the inspection VPC.
Add a static route for 0.0.0.0/0 in each spoke VPC pointing to the Transit Gateway.
questions.explanation: Without appliance mode, the Transit Gateway can send the forward and return legs of a flow to firewalls in different AZs, so each firewall sees only half the session. Appliance mode pins the flow to one AZ in the inspection VPC.
rationales: Correct. Appliance mode keeps the flow symmetric across AZs.
ECMP spreads traffic over more paths. It does not fix asymmetric routing through stateful appliances.
Peering is not transitive, so it cannot carry spoke-to-spoke traffic through an inspection VPC.
The spokes already reach the TGW. The problem is how the TGW picks the AZ in the inspection VPC.

questions.stem:
A company has peered Transit Gateways in eu-west-1 and us-east-1. VPCs in each Region are attached, and route propagation is enabled on all VPC attachments. Instances in eu-west-1 still cannot reach VPCs in us-east-1.

What should the network engineer do?
options: Enable route propagation for the peering attachment on both Transit Gateway route tables.
Add static routes for the remote Region's CIDRs that point to the peering attachment in each Transit Gateway route table.
Create a Direct Connect gateway and associate both Transit Gateways with it so that routes are exchanged.
Enable dynamic routing with BGP on the peering attachment.
questions.explanation: Transit Gateway peering supports only static routes. Each side needs static routes for the remote CIDRs that point at the peering attachment, and the VPC route tables must also send that traffic to the local TGW.
rationales: Propagation does not work over TGW peering attachments.
Correct. Peering attachments carry only static routes.
A DX gateway is for on-premises connectivity. It is not a way to exchange routes between peered TGWs.
BGP is not supported on TGW peering attachments.

questions.stem:
A bank runs payment systems in AWS that need the highest Direct Connect resiliency AWS offers. Its data center has a single Direct Connect location nearby, but a second location is available in another metro area.

Which connectivity design meets the requirement?
options: Two Direct Connect connections on separate devices at the nearby location.
One Direct Connect connection at each location, with no backup.
Separate Direct Connect connections terminating on separate devices at both locations.
One Direct Connect connection with a Site-to-Site VPN as the only backup.
questions.explanation: The maximum resiliency model uses separate connections on separate devices in more than one location and carries the 99.99% SLA. Single-location designs cannot survive a location failure.
rationales: That is the development and test model. It offers no protection against losing the location.
That matches the high resiliency model (99.9%), not maximum resiliency.
Correct. Redundant devices at more than one location is maximum resiliency.
VPN is a useful low-cost backup, but it is not the highest-resiliency DX design.

questions.stem:
A Transit Gateway has a Direct Connect gateway attachment and a Site-to-Site VPN attachment. Both advertise the on-premises prefix 10.50.0.0/16 to AWS. The team wants the VPN to carry traffic only if Direct Connect fails.

What must the team do to get this behavior?
options: Prepend the AS path on the VPN BGP session so the TGW prefers the Direct Connect route.
Nothing more. The Transit Gateway prefers the Direct Connect route for the same prefix and uses the VPN as backup.
Add a static route for 10.50.0.0/16 that points to the VPN attachment.
Turn off route propagation from the Direct Connect gateway attachment.
questions.explanation: For the same prefix, Transit Gateway prefers routes from a Direct Connect gateway over VPN routes, so the VPN is already the backup. A static route would override both propagated routes and force the opposite of what is wanted.
rationales: AS-path prepending is not needed to make DX preferred, because TGW already prefers DX for equal prefixes.
Correct. TGW route evaluation already prefers DX over VPN for the same prefix.
Static routes beat propagated routes, so this would force all traffic onto the VPN.
Removing DX propagation would send traffic over the VPN all the time.

questions.stem:
Applications in a data center must resolve records in a Route 53 private hosted zone associated with a shared-services VPC. The data center connects to AWS over Direct Connect and runs its own DNS servers.

Which solution meets the requirement?
options: Create a Route 53 VPC Resolver outbound endpoint and a forwarding rule for the private zone.
Make the private hosted zone public and restrict it with a resolver query log.
Create a Route 53 VPC Resolver inbound endpoint in the VPC and configure conditional forwarders on the on-premises DNS servers to its IP addresses.
Point on-premises clients directly at the VPC base address +2 over Direct Connect.
questions.explanation: Inbound endpoints give on-premises resolvers IP addresses in the VPC to forward queries to, and they answer from private hosted zones associated with that VPC. Outbound endpoints serve the opposite direction.
rationales: Outbound endpoints let VPC workloads query on-premises DNS, not the reverse.
Making internal records public exposes them and is not needed.
Correct. On-premises forwarders send queries to the inbound endpoint.
The +2 resolver is reachable only from inside the VPC, not from on-premises networks.

questions.stem:
A company has 60 workload accounts. Every VPC must resolve names in corp.example.internal, which are hosted on on-premises DNS servers reachable over a Transit Gateway. The team wants to manage DNS forwarding in one place.

Which approach meets these requirements with the least operational effort?
options: Create outbound endpoints and forwarding rules in each of the 60 accounts.
Run BIND forwarders on EC2 in each VPC and set them in DHCP option sets.
Create an inbound endpoint in a networking account and point all VPCs' DHCP option sets at it.
Create an outbound endpoint and forwarding rule in a central networking account, share the rule through AWS RAM, and associate it with each VPC.
questions.explanation: Resolver forwarding rules can be shared with other accounts through RAM. Spoke VPCs then use the central outbound endpoint without running their own, so DNS forwarding is managed in one place.
rationales: This works but duplicates endpoints and rules 60 times.
Self-managed DNS servers add patching and availability work.
Inbound endpoints receive queries from outside the VPC. They do not forward VPC queries to on-premises.
Correct. One endpoint plus a RAM-shared rule gives central management.

questions.stem:
A SaaS provider must let hundreds of customers reach its API from the customers' own VPCs without going over the internet. Many customers use 10.0.0.0/16, the same range as the provider's VPC, and the provider must not have network access into customer VPCs.

Which solution should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Publish the API as a VPC endpoint service behind a Network Load Balancer and have customers create interface endpoints through AWS PrivateLink.
Peer the provider VPC with each customer VPC.
Attach each customer VPC to the provider's Transit Gateway through AWS RAM.
Set up a Site-to-Site VPN from each customer VPC to the provider.
questions.explanation: PrivateLink presents the service as an interface endpoint inside each consumer VPC. It works across overlapping CIDRs and gives only one-way access to that service.
rationales: Correct. PrivateLink is built for exposing a service to many consumers privately.
Peering is not possible between VPCs with overlapping CIDRs and would give broad network access.
Overlapping CIDRs break TGW routing, and a TGW would allow two-way network reachability.
VPN tunnels per customer are hard to operate, and overlapping ranges would still need NAT.

questions.stem:
VPC A is peered with VPC B, and VPC B is peered with VPC C. Route tables in all three VPCs have routes for their peers. An instance in VPC A cannot reach an instance in VPC C.

What is the reason?
options: Security groups cannot reference instances in peered VPCs.
VPC peering does not support transitive routing, so A cannot reach C through B.
Peering connections require a Transit Gateway in VPC B.

Warm standby with a scaled-down copy of the whole stack running in the recovery Region

Which two changes most reduce latency and database load? (Select two.)
